fuentes/tablillas-arcaicas-de-uruk/resum.texto: Thousands of accounting tablets and fragments found at Uruk, with numerical and pictographic signs that record mainly goods and rations. With them the documented history of writing in Mesopotamia begins; among them are also lexical lists that scribes went on copying for centuries.

fuentes/tablillas-arcaicas-de-uruk/por_q.texto: They show that writing was born as an administrative tool and allow the study of the organization of Uruk's institutions before there were narrative texts.

fuentes/tablillas-arcaicas-de-uruk/leer..texto: Uruk IV tablets with photographs and transliteration, at the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative

fuentes/tablillas-de-jemdet-nasr/resumen.texto: Proto-cuneiform administrative texts from the Jemdet Nasr period, found at the mound of that name, recording goods and rations with a sign system more advanced than that of Uruk IV.

fuentes/tablillas-de-jemdet-nasr/por_que.texto: They attest the spread of writing beyond Uruk in the last century of the 4th millennium BC.

fuentes/tablillas-de-jemdet-nasr/leer.0..texto: Jemdet Nasr tablets with photographs and transliteration, at the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative

fuentes/tablillas-de-fara/resumen.texto: Tablets found at Shuruppak (Tell Fara) from the Early Dynastic III period. They contain accounts, land contracts and lexical lists, and also literary texts.

fuentes/tablillas-de-fara/por_que_import.texto: They are one of the largest Sumerian archives before Sargon and show the economy of a city of central Sumer in the mid-third millennium.

fuentes/tablillas-de-fara/leer.0.titulo.texto: Fara tablets with photographs and transliteration, at the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative

fuentes/tablillas-de-abu-salabikh/resume.texto: Tablets found at Abu Salabikh with administrative and lexical texts and literary compositions: a hymnal (the Zame Hymns), the Hymn to the Temple of Kesh and the Instructions of Shuruppak, among the oldest known literary works.

fuentes/tablillas-de-abu-salabikh/por_qu.texto: They show that literary genres thought to belong to the second millennium BC were already circulating in the Early Dynastic III period.

fuentes/tablillas-de-abu-salabikh/leer.0.texto: Abu Salabikh tablets with photographs and transliteration, at the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative

fuentes/himnos-de-zame/resumen.texto: Collection of 70 Sumerian hymns from the Early Dynastic period found at Abu Salabikh. Its conventional title comes from the formula zame, “praise.” It is the oldest known hymn collection from Mesopotamia; there are no copies outside Abu Salabikh.

fuentes/himnos-de-zame/por_que_importa.texto: They are the basis on which temple liturgy before the Akkadian period is studied.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-shuruppak/autor.texto: Anonymous (attributed within the text itself to Shuruppak, son of Ubara-Tutu)

fuentes/instrucciones-de-shuruppak/resum.texto: Sumerian wisdom text whose advice is put in the mouth of Shuruppak, who speaks to his son Ziusudra. Copies survive from Abu Salabikh and from later periods. Together with the Hymn to the Temple of Kesh, it is one of the oldest known literary works.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-shuruppak/por_q.texto: It shows the values and domestic morality that Sumerian tradition associated with a remote age, and it served as a model for the wisdom genre.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-shuruppak/leer..texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/himno-al-templo-de-kesh/titulo.texto: Hymn to the Temple of Kesh

fuentes/himno-al-templo-de-kesh/resumen.texto: Sumerian hymn to the temple of Nintud at Kesh, also called the Liturgy to Nintud, preserved on tablets from Abu Salabikh and in later copies. It praises the temple and its goddess, and mentions its relation to the creation of man and woman.

fuentes/himno-al-templo-de-kesh/por_que_.texto: It is one of the oldest literary compositions that survive.

fuentes/himno-al-templo-de-kesh/leer.0.t.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/estela-de-los-buitres/resumen.texto: Stele of Eannatum of Lagash commemorating his victory over Ush of Umma, with reliefs of the battle and a long text on the war over the border. It is considered the oldest known war monument. Seven fragments were found at Tello in the 1880s and are in the Louvre (one came from the British Museum in 1932).

fuentes/estela-de-los-buitres/por_que_im.texto: It is the main source on the war between Lagash and Umma in the version of Lagash, which presents Ningirsu as the injured party.

fuentes/estela-de-los-buitres/leer.0.tit.texto: Corpus of royal inscriptions of Lagash, Gudea and Ur III in ORACC (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/cono-de-entemena/resumen.texto: Clay cone of Entemena of Lagash with an account of the dispute with Umma over the Gu-Edin: the arbitration of Mesilim of Kish, the violation of the border by Ush and Enakalle, the victory of Eannatum and the deeds of Entemena against Il of Umma. It is the main source on the history of that border.

fuentes/cono-de-entemena/por_que_importa.texto: It is the Lagashite version of a conflict we know only through Lagash; the partiality of the source must be taken into account.

fuentes/reformas-de-urukagina/titulo.texto: Inscriptions of the reforms of Urukagina

fuentes/reformas-de-urukagina/resumen.texto: Inscriptions of Urukagina of Lagash, on clay cones and tablets, which list abuses by his predecessors and reforms that he says he made, among them limits on taxes and on exactions by officials and priests. There is no solid evidence of a single reform or of a law code. The Sumerian word amargi appears in them, interpreted as “freedom” by some and debated by others.

fuentes/reformas-de-urukagina/por_que_im.texto: They are cited as one of the oldest texts of social reform; specialists debate their real scope and what they say about the system of government.

fuentes/cilindros-de-gudea/resumen.texto: Two clay cylinders of Gudea of Lagash with an extensive Sumerian hymn on the reconstruction of the Eninnu, the temple of Ningirsu at Girsu, including a dream and the inauguration ceremony. Found at Tello.

fuentes/cilindros-de-gudea/por_que_impor.texto: They are among the longest known Sumerian texts and a central source on religion and temple building at the end of the third millennium.

fuentes/cilindros-de-gudea/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/estatuas-de-gudea/resumen.texto: Corpus of 24 to 27 diorite statues of Gudea of Lagash, many with inscriptions naming the temples where he placed them and the materials he brought from distant places; the diorite came from Magan. Most were found at Girsu (reinstalled in the Hellenistic palace), and others at Nippur and Tell Hammam; several are of unknown provenance, and some are suspected to be modern forgeries. They are in the Louvre and other museums.

fuentes/estatuas-de-gudea/por_que_import.texto: They document long-distance trade and the building program of the Second Dynasty of Lagash.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-sargon/titulo.texto: Royal inscriptions of Sargon of Akkad

fuentes/inscripciones-de-sargon/resumen.texto: Inscriptions of Sargon recounting his conquests: the victory over Lugalzagesi, the campaigns in Elam and Marhashi, the arrival at Tuttul and the year names. Many are known from Old Babylonian school copies made in Nippur and elsewhere.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-sargon/por_que_.texto: They are the basis for the historical reconstruction of his reign; as they are late copies, they must be used with caution.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-sargon/leer.0.t.texto: Corpus of royal inscriptions of Akkad in ORACC (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/obelisco-de-manishtushu/resumen.texto: Diorite monument with a long Akkadian inscription by Manishtushu on purchases of land for the crown, with the names of the sellers and of the officials who witnessed them. Its origin is unknown, and it is believed to come from Sippar; de Morgan found it at Susa in 1897, where it had been taken as booty in the second millennium.

fuentes/obelisco-de-manishtushu/por_que_.texto: It is a source on land ownership and on the Akkadian ruling group, the “sons of Akkad.”

fuentes/estela-de-naram-sin/resumen.texto: Stele of Naram-Sin with the victory over the Lullubi, which shows him on the mountain wearing a horned crown. It was at Sippar (its place of origin is unknown), and the Elamite king Shutruk-Nakhunte took it to Susa in the 12th century BC; today it is in the Louvre.

fuentes/estela-de-naram-sin/por_que_impo.texto: It is the best-known image of the Akkadian Empire and shows the cult of the deified king.

fuentes/estatua-de-bassetki/resumen.texto: Base with the lower part of a seated figure, of nearly pure copper cast by the lost-wax process, found at Bassetki, in northern Iraq, in 1974. Its inscription says that the statue stood at the gate of a palace of Naram-Sin and recounts the uprising of the cities against him, and that the people of Akkad asked the gods to make him a god of their city.

fuentes/estatua-de-bassetki/por_que_impo.texto: It is a direct source on the great revolt against Naram-Sin and on his deification.

fuentes/tratado-de-naram-sin-y-hita/titu.texto: Treaty between Naram-Sin of Akkad and Hita of Elam

fuentes/tratado-de-naram-sin-y-hita/resu.texto: Tablet found at Susa with an agreement between Naram-Sin and a king of Awan, identified with Hita (Khita), with an invocation of Elamite and Akkadian gods as witnesses. It is one of the oldest known treaties and one of the oldest texts in Elamite.

fuentes/tratado-de-naram-sin-y-hita/por_.texto: It shows that the Akkadian kings made pacts with neighbors, not only conquered them.

fuentes/maldicion-de-acad/soporte.texto: Poem of 280 lines, in Old Babylonian copies

fuentes/maldicion-de-acad/resumen.texto: Sumerian poem composed at the end of the third millennium, in the Ur III period, and preserved in Old Babylonian copies. It explains the fall of Akkad as the punishment of Enlil on Naram-Sin for his offense against the Ekur: the god sends the Gutians against the land. Current studies see a more gradual fall and attribute Naram-Sin's bad image in the south to his policy in Sumer.

fuentes/maldicion-de-acad/por_que_import.texto: It is the best-known example of a theological reading of a political disaster; it is not a reliable source on the reign of Naram-Sin.

fuentes/maldicion-de-acad/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/himnos-de-enheduanna/resumen.texto: A group of Sumerian poems, among them the Exaltation of Inanna, which Old Babylonian school tradition attributed to Enheduanna; they are known from copies of the 18th century BC, and their original authorship is debated among specialists.

fuentes/himnos-de-enheduanna/por_que_imp.texto: They are the basis for the idea of Enheduanna as the earliest named author in history, which some authorities accept and others doubt.

fuentes/himnos-de-enheduanna/leer.0.titu.texto: Exaltation of Inanna, English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/codigo-de-ur-nammu/resumen.texto: Collection of Sumerian laws of the Third Dynasty of Ur, attributed to Ur-Nammu (or to Shulgi). It is known from Old Babylonian copies from Nippur (Istanbul), Ur (Iraq Museum) and Sippar (Istanbul and the British Museum), and from a Ur III cylinder of unknown provenance (Schøyen collection). Its prologue mentions reforms of weights and measures and sets monetary penalties for crimes.

fuentes/codigo-de-ur-nammu/por_que_impor.texto: It is the oldest known law collection today, about three centuries older than that of Hammurabi, and it shows the casuistic model of law that Hammurabi's code continued.

fuentes/archivos-de-puzrish-dagan/autor.texto: Scribes of the Ur III state (anonymous)

fuentes/archivos-de-puzrish-dagan/resume.texto: Thousands of administrative tablets from Puzrish-Dagan (Drehem), which reached the antiquities market, recording the receipt and distribution of livestock and offerings under Shulgi, Amar-Sin, Shu-Sin and Ibbi-Sin. They also record the arrival of foreign envoys.

fuentes/archivos-de-puzrish-dagan/por_qu.texto: They are the most important source on the taxation and redistribution system of the Third Dynasty of Ur.

fuentes/archivos-de-puzrish-dagan/leer.0.texto: Puzrish-Dagan tablets with photographs and transliteration, at the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative

fuentes/archivos-de-umma-ur-iii/titulo.texto: Umma archives of the Third Dynasty of Ur

fuentes/archivos-de-umma-ur-iii/resumen.texto: More than 30,000 tablets from Umma, mostly administrative and economic records from the Ur III period, which show the affairs of a province.

fuentes/archivos-de-umma-ur-iii/por_que_.texto: They allow the affairs of an Ur III province to be reconstructed.

fuentes/archivos-de-umma-ur-iii/leer.0.t.texto: Umma tablets with photographs and transliteration, at the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative

fuentes/archivos-de-girsu-ur-iii/titulo.texto: Girsu archives of the Third Dynasty of Ur

fuentes/archivos-de-girsu-ur-iii/resumen.texto: Administrative tablets from Girsu, in the province of Lagash, from the Ur III period, with administrative records of the province of Lagash. According to the known archives, the economy of the province of Umma was equal to a third of that of Lagash.

fuentes/archivos-de-girsu-ur-iii/por_que.texto: They show the state management of Ur III in one of its provinces.

fuentes/archivos-de-girsu-ur-iii/leer.0..texto: Girsu tablets with photographs and transliteration, at the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative

fuentes/lamento-por-ur/resumen.texto: Sumerian lament composed around the time of the fall of Ur to the Elamites and the end of the Third Dynasty (c. 2000 BC). It laments the destruction of the city in the voice of its goddess Ningal.

fuentes/lamento-por-ur/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main literary source on the fall of Ur, and it should be read as a poem, not as a chronicle.

fuentes/lamento-por-ur/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/lamento-por-sumer-y-ur/resumen.texto: Another of the five laments for Sumerian cities, also on the ruin of Ur and of the cities of Sumer. It says that Shimashki and Elam settled in the country and that Ibbi-Suen was led away in chains to the land of Elam; it does not name Kindattu.

fuentes/lamento-por-sumer-y-ur/por_que_i.texto: Together with the Lament for Ur, it is the main literary source on the end of the Third Dynasty.

fuentes/lamento-por-sumer-y-ur/leer.0.ti.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/gilgamesh-y-aga/resumen.texto: Old Babylonian Sumerian poem about the siege of Uruk by Kish when Gilgamesh refuses to submit to Agga; it ends with the defeat of Agga and the loss of Kish's hegemony. It is the only one of the five Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh without mythological elements.

fuentes/gilgamesh-y-aga/por_que_importa.texto: It is the narrative source for the rivalry between Kish and Uruk, a tradition with no contemporary support.

fuentes/gilgamesh-y-aga/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/gilgamesh-enkidu-y-el-inframundo.texto: Sumerian poem in which Gilgamesh helps the goddess Inanna and then descends to the netherworld to retrieve fallen objects; it is probably the oldest of the Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh. Its ending is the origin of the twelfth tablet of the Akkadian epic.
It is one of the Sumerian sources of the Gilgamesh legend that later passed into the epic.
English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/enmerkar-y-el-senor-de-aratta/ti.texto: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta

fuentes/enmerkar-y-el-senor-de-aratta/re.texto: Sumerian narrative composed in the Neo-Sumerian period (21st century BC), about the conflict between Enmerkar of Uruk and the lord of Aratta. It contains a passage on the “confusion of tongues” and presents Enmerkar as the inventor of writing.

fuentes/enmerkar-y-el-senor-de-aratta/po.texto: It is evidence of how Ur III scribes reworked the past of Uruk, not of events of the third millennium.

fuentes/enmerkar-y-el-senor-de-aratta/le.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/lugalbanda-en-la-cueva-de-la-mon.texto: Sumerian poem about Lugalbanda, a soldier in Enmerkar's army against Aratta, who falls ill and is left behind in a cave in the mountains. It is the first part of a cycle of two poems.
A source of the legend of Lugalbanda, a king in the Uruk tradition.
English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/lugalbanda-y-el-pajaro-anzud/res.texto: Sumerian poem about Lugalbanda and the bird Anzud, which grants him supernatural speed to rejoin Enmerkar's army. It is the second part of the Lugalbanda cycle.

fuentes/lugalbanda-y-el-pajaro-anzud/por.texto: It completes the legend of Lugalbanda as the protagonist of the Aratta cycle.

fuentes/lugalbanda-y-el-pajaro-anzud/lee.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/debate-entre-oveja-y-grano/titul.texto: Debate between the Sheep and the Grain

fuentes/debate-entre-oveja-y-grano/resum.texto: Sumerian dispute and creation myth, written on clay tablets toward the end of the third millennium BC, in which livestock and grain compete to show which is more useful.

fuentes/debate-entre-oveja-y-grano/por_q.texto: An example of the Sumerian dispute genre.

fuentes/debate-entre-oveja-y-grano/leer..texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/debate-entre-invierno-y-verano/r.texto: Sumerian creation myth of the dispute genre, which sets Emesh (summer) and Enten (winter) against each other before Enlil; it was written on clay tablets toward the end of the third millennium BC.

fuentes/debate-entre-invierno-y-verano/p.texto: An example of the Sumerian dispute genre.

fuentes/debate-entre-invierno-y-verano/l.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/debate-entre-ave-y-pez/titulo.texto: Debate between the Bird and the Fish

fuentes/debate-entre-ave-y-pez/resumen.texto: Sumerian dispute dated to the end of the third millennium BC, between a bird and a fish that boast of their virtues before a judge.

fuentes/debate-entre-ave-y-pez/por_que_i.texto: An example of the Sumerian dispute genre.

fuentes/debate-entre-ave-y-pez/leer.0.ti.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/debate-entre-azada-y-arado/titul.texto: Debate between the Hoe and the Plough

fuentes/debate-entre-azada-y-arado/resum.texto: Sumerian dispute of 196 lines dated to the Third Dynasty of Ur, in which two farming implements compete for usefulness. The text was reconstructed by M. Civil in the 1960s.

fuentes/debate-entre-azada-y-arado/por_q.texto: An example of the Sumerian dispute genre.

fuentes/debate-entre-azada-y-arado/leer..texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/tablilla-de-kish/resumen.texto: Limestone tablet found at Kish with undeciphered pictographic signs, perhaps related to proto-cuneiform; it is dated to the Late Uruk period. The original is in the Iraq Museum and the Ashmolean has a copy. It is not proven that it was an administrative text.

fuentes/tablilla-de-kish/por_que_importa.texto: It shows that writing spread from Uruk to other cities.

fuentes/woolley-cementerio-real-de-ur/ti.texto: Excavations at Ur, vol. II: The Royal Cemetery

fuentes/woolley-cementerio-real-de-ur/re.texto: Woolley's report on the Predynastic and Sargonic tombs excavated in the Royal Cemetery of Ur between 1926 and 1931, published by the joint expedition of the British Museum and the University of Pennsylvania. Its dating and its interpretation of the attendant burials have since been revised.

fuentes/woolley-cementerio-real-de-ur/po.texto: It is the fundamental excavation report on the cemetery; Pollock and others have revised its chronology.

fuentes/kuhrt-el-antiguo-oriente-proximo.texto: The Ancient Near East, c. 3000–330 BC
Two-volume history of the ancient Near East with a selection of ancient texts in translation. It is cited as a synthesis work in articles on Mesopotamia.
A reference academic synthesis with the sources in translation.

fuentes/crawford-el-mundo-sumerio/resume.texto: Collective work on the history, language, art and society of Sumer, edited by Harriet Crawford and published by Routledge.

fuentes/crawford-el-mundo-sumerio/por_qu.texto: A recent academic synthesis on the Sumerian world.

fuentes/roaf-atlas-cultural-de-mesopotam.texto: Cultural Atlas of Mesopotamia and the Ancient Near East
Illustrated atlas of the history and archaeology of Mesopotamia and neighboring regions, published by Equinox and Facts on File.
A reference for the location and chronology of sites and kingdoms.

fuentes/estela-de-la-victoria-de-utu-hen.texto: Stele, known from a copy of the Isin period

Inscription of Utu-hengal of Uruk recounting his victory over the Gutians and their king Tirigan, which according to the text was commissioned by Enlil. A copy made in the Isin dynasty survives, today in the Louvre.
It is the direct source for the end of Gutian rule and the basis for the tradition of Utu-hengal as a Sumerian hero; it is propaganda text written from the victor's perspective.
Poem of Utu-hegal, English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/inscripciones-de-ur-nanshe/sopor.texto: Votive plaques and a perforated relief

fuentes/inscripciones-de-ur-nanshe/resum.texto: Inscriptions of Ur-Nanshe of Lagash on plaques that show him with his family and court, and on the perforated relief. They name his works on canals and temples, among them the temple of Ningirsu at Girsu and that of Nanshe at Nina, and the capture of Pabilgagaltuku of Umma.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-ur-nanshe/por_q.texto: They are the direct source for the beginning of the First Dynasty of Lagash.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-eannatum/resume.texto: Inscriptions of Eannatum of Lagash, which say that he conquered Elam, Urua, Umma and Ur, that he repulsed Akshak, and that he took the title “king of Kish” and demanded tribute as far as Mari. They are accounts by the king himself, without independent confirmation.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-eannatum/por_qu.texto: They are the basis for the image of Eannatum as the creator of one of the first extensive dominions in Mesopotamia, and they must be read as royal propaganda.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-enshakushanna/s.texto: Stone bowl fragments found at Nippur

fuentes/inscripciones-de-enshakushanna/r.texto: Inscriptions of Enshakushanna of Uruk, on bowl fragments dedicated to Enlil, which record his attack on Kish and Akshak and the capture of Enbi-Ishtar, king of Kish. A dedicatory tablet in his name is in the Hermitage.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-enshakushanna/p.texto: They are the source of his claim to hegemony over Sumer, which the Sumerian King List records only as a reign of 60 years.

fuentes/cono-del-pacto-de-hermandad/titu.texto: Cones of Entemena from the Emush temple (brotherhood pact)

fuentes/cono-del-pacto-de-hermandad/resu.texto: Clay cones of Entemena of Lagash that record the construction of the Emush temple for Inanna and Lugal-emush and the brotherhood pact with Lugal-kinishe-dudu of Uruk. They are attributed to Tell al-Madineh (Bad-tibira) on the basis of illegal excavations, and their exact provenance has been debated.

fuentes/cono-del-pacto-de-hermandad/por_.texto: It is the only source for the alliance between Lagash and Uruk, which is absent from the cone of Entemena on the border.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-rimush/resumen.texto: Inscriptions of Rimush of Akkad, among them the dedication of a statue of meteoric iron to Enlil. They recount that he had to reconquer Ur, Umma, Adab, Lagash, Der and Kazallu from rebel governors, and that he defeated Adab and Zabalam by capturing Meskigal, governor of Adab.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-rimush/por_que_.texto: They are the source for the rebellions of his reign, written by the king himself.

fuentes/inscripcion-estandar-de-manishtu.texto: Statue fragments and Old Babylonian copies

Inscription known from at least eight examples: statue fragments from Nippur, Sippar, Susa and Khafajah, and Old Babylonian copies on tablets from Nippur and Ur. It says that, having defeated Anshan and Sherihum, he had his ships cross the Lower Sea, and that thirty-two cities on the other side gathered to fight him and were defeated.
It is the source for the campaigns of Manishtushu; that the cities across the sea were Magan is an interpretation.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-ur-nammu/resume.texto: Inscriptions and year names of Ur-Nammu that recount his works (the ziggurat of Ur, the Iturungal canal) and his victories, among them one over a coalition led by Kutik-Inshushinak. Seventeen year names are known for his eighteen years of reign, in uncertain order.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-ur-nammu/por_qu.texto: They are the direct source for the reign of Ur-Nammu, apart from the poem about his death.

fuentes/estela-de-ur-nammu/resumen.texto: Limestone stele with reliefs on both faces, found in fragments in 1925 by Woolley in the precinct of Nanna at Ur; part of it is in the Penn Museum. Its reconstruction is debated.

fuentes/estela-de-ur-nammu/por_que_impor.texto: It is the most complete image of the works of the founding king of Ur III, but its fragments do not allow a secure reading.

fuentes/muerte-de-ur-nammu/soporte.texto: About nine fragments, Old Babylonian copies

fuentes/muerte-de-ur-nammu/resumen.texto: Sumerian poem about the death of Ur-Nammu on the battlefield, the abandonment of his army and his descent to the netherworld. The passage on the death is damaged and vague and metaphorical.

fuentes/muerte-de-ur-nammu/por_que_impor.texto: It is the source for the claim that Ur-Nammu died in combat, written long after the fact, and that he was not deified.

fuentes/muerte-de-ur-nammu/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/dedicatoria-de-taram-uram/resume.texto: Dedication of Taram-Uram, who presents herself as the daughter of Apil-kin, lugal of Mari, and the daughter-in-law of Ur-Nammu.

fuentes/dedicatoria-de-taram-uram/por_qu.texto: It is the source for her origin and for the marriage alliance between Mari and Ur.

fuentes/nombres-de-ano-de-ur-iii/titulo.texto: Year names of the Third Dynasty of Ur

fuentes/nombres-de-ano-de-ur-iii/autor.texto: Scribes of the Third Dynasty of Ur (anonymous)

fuentes/nombres-de-ano-de-ur-iii/resumen.texto: The names by which the kings of Ur III dated their documents: each year was named after an event of the previous year, such as a work, a victory or a reform. Complete lists are known for Amar-Sin, Shu-Sin and Ibbi-Sin, and the 48 of Shulgi.

fuentes/nombres-de-ano-de-ur-iii/por_que.texto: They are the internal chronology of the kingdom and the source for its campaigns, walls and reforms.

fuentes/estatua-de-ebih-il/resumen.texto: Statue of a worshipper, the superintendent Ebih-Il of Mari, of gypsum with inlays of shell, schist and lapis lazuli, dedicated to “Ishtar the virile.” Parrot found it in 1934 in the temple of Ishtar at Mari, and it is in the Louvre.

fuentes/estatua-de-ebih-il/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the few direct sources for the second kingdom of Mari.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-puzur-inshushin.texto: Inscriptions of Puzur-Inshushinak found at Susa, in Akkadian and in Linear Elamite, the script he promoted. Some blocks carry separate texts in the two languages.
They are the direct source for his reign and most of what survives in Linear Elamite.

fuentes/monumentos-de-blau/resumen.texto: Two inscribed stones, bought in 1886 near Uruk and now in the British Museum, usually taken to be archaic boundary markers. They are dated between Uruk III and Early Dynastic I: some authors place them around 3100 BC on the basis of the form of the writing, others around 2700 BC.

fuentes/monumentos-de-blau/por_que_impor.texto: They show early writing applied to land ownership.

fuentes/estela-de-ushumgal/resumen.texto: Archaic Sumerian stele, perhaps from Umma and now in the Metropolitan Museum, which seems to record a transfer of land. One figure bears the label “Ushumgal, pab-sheh priest of Shara,” and on the other side is his daughter.

fuentes/estela-de-ushumgal/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the oldest testimonies of written transfers of property.

fuentes/vaso-de-entemena/soporte.texto: Silver tripod vessel with copper feet

fuentes/vaso-de-entemena/resumen.texto: Silver vessel with copper feet, believed to have been dedicated to Ningirsu, engraved with Anzud, the lion-headed eagle, grasping two lions. In 1910 L. W. King described it as the best example of Sumerian metalwork found up to that time.

fuentes/vaso-de-entemena/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the level of goldsmithing in Lagash in the time of Entemena.

fuentes/estatua-de-iddi-ilum/resumen.texto: Headless statue of a worshipper, of Iddi-ilum, shakkanakku of Mari, whom the inscription dedicates to Ishtar or Inanna. Parrot found it in the royal palace of Mari, and it is in the Louvre.

fuentes/estatua-de-iddi-ilum/por_que_imp.texto: It is a direct source on the shakkanakku of Mari under the Third Dynasty of Ur.

fuentes/relieve-de-anubanini/resumen.texto: Lullubi rock relief near Sarpol-e Zahab, in the province of Kermanshah, in Iran, dated either to the Akkadian period (c. 2300 BC) or to the Isin-Larsa period (early second millennium BC). Lullubi reliefs are the oldest in Iran.

fuentes/relieve-de-anubanini/por_que_imp.texto: It shows a Lullubi king depicted as Naram-Sin in his stele.

fuentes/cilindro-de-barton/resumen.texto: Clay cylinder with a Sumerian creation myth, from the middle or end of the third millennium; J. G. Westenholz dates it to around 2400 BC (Early Dynastic III). It is in the Penn Museum.

fuentes/cilindro-de-barton/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the oldest Sumerian creation myths.

fuentes/inscripcion-del-tummal/soporte.texto: Sixteen copies (12 from Nippur, 3 from Ur)

fuentes/inscripcion-del-tummal/resumen.texto: A text regarded as one of the Babylonian chronicles, written in the time of Ishbi-Erra, which lists the rulers who built the temple of Enlil in Nippur and the temples of Ninlil at the Tummal. Sixteen slightly different copies survive.

fuentes/inscripcion-del-tummal/por_que_i.texto: It is later tradition about the succession of kings who looked after the cult of Nippur and of Ninlil.

fuentes/inscripcion-del-tummal/leer.0.ti.texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/tablilla-dinastica-de-scheil/res.texto: Cuneiform text with a variant of the Sumerian King List, which Scheil translated in 1911 after buying it from a private collection in France; it was said to come from Susa. It dates to the early second millennium BC.

fuentes/tablilla-dinastica-de-scheil/por.texto: It serves to compare the Sumerian King List with a parallel version from a period after the events.

fuentes/correspondencia-de-los-reyes-de-.texto: Correspondence of the Kings of Ur
24 literary letters in Old Babylonian copies

Collection of 24 literary letters in Sumerian attributed to kings of Ur III, among them letters between Ibbi-Sin and Ishbi-Erra. They are known mainly from copies of c. 1800–1600 BC, and their date of composition and historical accuracy are debated; some regard them as apocryphal.
It is the source for the last years of Ur III, to be read with the caution due to a school collection.

fuentes/enmerkar-y-en-suhgir-ana/resumen.texto: Sumerian narrative, the second of four in the cycle of the contests of Aratta against Enmerkar of Uruk and his successor Lugalbanda. It continues “Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta.”

fuentes/enmerkar-y-en-suhgir-ana/por_que.texto: It completes the Aratta cycle as a story about the past of Uruk, not as a document.

fuentes/enmerkar-y-en-suhgir-ana/leer.0..texto: English translation from ETCSL (copy on the Internet Archive)

fuentes/muerte-de-gilgamesh/resumen.texto: Sumerian poem about the death of Gilgamesh, who learns that Enlil destined him to a mortal life, although he gave him kingship and heroism, and it ends with a lament. Kramer reconstructed it and published his edition in 1944.

fuentes/muerte-de-gilgamesh/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the Sumerian sources of the Gilgamesh legend, with no value as a historical document.

fuentes/cancion-de-la-azada/resumen.texto: Sumerian creation myth written on tablets of the last century of the third millennium BC. It is one of the Sumerian disputes, together with the debates between the sheep and the grain or between winter and summer.

fuentes/cancion-de-la-azada/por_que_impo.texto: An example of the Sumerian dispute genre.

fuentes/descenso-de-inanna-al-inframundo.texto: Descent of Inanna to the Netherworld

Sumerian myth in which Inanna descends to the netherworld to overthrow her sovereign Ereshkigal, dies, is brought back to life through the intervention of Enki, and must hand over another being in exchange; she chooses Dumuzi. There is also a later Akkadian version.
It is the main source for the myth of Inanna and Dumuzi, known from Old Babylonian copies.

fuentes/genesis-de-eridu/resumen.texto: Sumerian text on the creation of humanity by the gods, the origin of the first cities and of kingship, and the flood, preserved in three fragments of different versions, one of them found at Nippur. The antediluvian kings and Ziusudra of the Sumerian King List belong to the same tradition.

fuentes/genesis-de-eridu/por_que_importa.texto: It is later tradition, not a document from the period it narrates.

fuentes/leyenda-de-naram-sin-y-los-cuteo.texto: Old Babylonian, Middle Babylonian and Standard versions

Akkadian literary work about Naram-Sin and the Gutians, in Old Babylonian, Middle Babylonian and Standard versions, with about 1500 years of literary life. It is a moral tale with a didactic purpose and not a historical account.
It helps distinguish between what Naram-Sin's inscriptions say and what later tradition told about him.

fuentes/rey-de-la-batalla/soporte.texto: Five manuscripts: two from Amarna, one from Hattusa, one from Assur and one from Nineveh

fuentes/rey-de-la-batalla/resumen.texto: Akkadian epic account of Sargon's campaign against Purushanda, in the highlands of Anatolia, and its king Nur-Daggal, in defense of his merchants. It is one of three legends of the kings of Akkad that continued to be copied in the Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian periods.

fuentes/rey-de-la-batalla/por_que_import.texto: It is a tradition used to contrast the legend of Sargon with his inscriptions.

fuentes/cronica-de-los-reyes-antiguos/re.texto: Babylonian chronicle that begins with Sargon of Akkad and runs down to Agum III (c. 1500 BC). It is put together from omen apodoses, passages of the Weidner Chronicle and year names of kings, and it recounts the fall of Sargon as a punishment by Marduk.

fuentes/cronica-de-los-reyes-antiguos/po.texto: It serves to attribute the later legends about Sargon and Naram-Sin and to distinguish them from the facts.

fuentes/cronica-de-los-reyes-antiguos/le.texto: Translation of the Chronicle of the Ancient Kings (ABC 20), on Livius

fuentes/frayne-rime-2/soporte.texto: Book (The Royal Inscriptions of Mesopotamia, Early Periods, vol. 2)

fuentes/frayne-rime-2/resumen.texto: Edition of the royal inscriptions of the kings of Akkad and of the Gutian rulers, with translation and commentary, published by the University of Toronto Press.

fuentes/frayne-rime-2/por_que_importa.texto: It is the reference edition of the inscriptions of Sargon, Rimush, Manishtushu, Naram-Sin and Erridupizir.

fuentes/frayne-rime-3-2/soporte.texto: Book (The Royal Inscriptions of Mesopotamia, Early Periods, vol. 3/2)

fuentes/frayne-rime-3-2/resumen.texto: Edition of the royal inscriptions of the kings of the Third Dynasty of Ur, published by the University of Toronto Press.

fuentes/frayne-rime-3-2/por_que_importa.texto: It is the reference edition of the inscriptions of Ur-Nammu and his successors.

fuentes/edzard-rime-3-1/soporte.texto: Book (The Royal Inscriptions of Mesopotamia, Early Periods, vol. 3/1)

fuentes/edzard-rime-3-1/resumen.texto: Edition of the inscriptions of Gudea and of the other rulers of the Second Dynasty of Lagash, published by the University of Toronto Press.

fuentes/edzard-rime-3-1/por_que_importa.texto: It is the reference edition of the inscriptions of Gudea.

fuentes/michalowski-correspondencia-de-l.texto: The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur: An Epistolary History of an Ancient Mesopotamian Kingdom
Edition and study of the literary letters attributed to the kings of Ur III, published by Eisenbrauns.
It is the reference edition of the correspondence, with its problems of reliability.

fuentes/westenholz-leyendas-de-los-reyes.texto: Legends of the Kings of Akkade
Edition, with study, of the literary texts about the kings of Akkad, published by Eisenbrauns.
It helps tell apart what is legend from what is attested in the inscriptions of the period.

fuentes/steinkeller-puzur-inshushinak/ti.texto: Puzur-Inšušinak at Susa: A Decisive Episode of Early Elamite History, Reconsidered

fuentes/steinkeller-puzur-inshushinak/re.texto: Study by Steinkeller of the reign of Puzur-Inshushinak, included in the volume Susa and Elam, edited by Katrien De Graef and Jan Tavernier. It proposes a shorter chronology for this period.

fuentes/steinkeller-puzur-inshushinak/po.texto: It helps date the reign of Puzur-Inshushinak in relation to Akkad and to Ur III.

fuentes/weiss-genesis-y-colapso-del-terc.texto: The Genesis and Collapse of the Third Millennium North Mesopotamian Civilization

Article by Weiss and colleagues, published in Science in 1993, which proposes that a widespread drought around 2200 BC caused the abandonment of Tell Leilan and other sites in northern Mesopotamia and contributed to the collapse of the Akkadian Empire.
It is the origin of the climate hypothesis that other specialists debate.

fuentes/weiss-siete-generaciones/titulo.texto: Seven Generations Since the Fall of Akkad

fuentes/weiss-siete-generaciones/resumen.texto: Volume edited by Harvey Weiss on the collapse of the third millennium and its consequences, which develops the 4.2 ka drought hypothesis.

fuentes/weiss-siete-generaciones/por_que.texto: It brings together the case for that hypothesis.

fuentes/kramer-muerte-de-ur-nammu/titulo.texto: The Death of Ur-Nammu and His Descent to the Netherworld

fuentes/kramer-muerte-de-ur-nammu/resume.texto: Study and edition of the Sumerian poem on the death of Ur-Nammu, published in the Journal of Cuneiform Studies.

fuentes/kramer-muerte-de-ur-nammu/por_qu.texto: It is the classic edition of the poem.

fuentes/sharlach-un-buey-propio/titulo.texto: A Bull of His Own: Royal Wives and Religion at the Court of the Third Dynasty of Ur

fuentes/sharlach-un-buey-propio/resumen.texto: Study of the royal wives of Ur III and their religious role, with a historical introduction to the reigns of Ur-Nammu and Shulgi.

fuentes/sharlach-un-buey-propio/por_que_.texto: It is useful for the queens and diplomatic marriages of Ur III.

personas/ubara-tutu/resumen.texto: Last antediluvian king of Shuruppak according to some versions of the Sumerian King List, which gives him a reign of 18,600 years. A figure of tradition; there are no contemporary inscriptions of his.

personas/ziusudra/resumen.texto: King of Shuruppak who survives the flood in the Sumerian tradition, known only from texts of the second millennium BC and later. No contemporary attestation.

personas/etana/resumen.texto: Thirteenth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, which calls him “the shepherd who ascended to heaven.” Known only from the List and from the later legend that bears his name; there are no inscriptions of his own.

personas/zuqaqip/resumen.texto: Ninth king of the First Dynasty of Kish in the Sumerian King List, with a reign of 900 years. His name does not appear in Early Dynastic texts, so he probably did not exist.

personas/dumuzid-el-pescador/resumen.texto: King of Uruk, from Kuara, according to the Sumerian King List, which gives him a reign of 100 years (110 in one manuscript). One single manuscript adds a phrase that the standard translation reads as “he captured Enmebaragesi with his own hand”; a more recent reading reverses the roles. It is a debated tradition.

personas/lugalbanda/resumen.texto: Third king of the First Dynasty of Uruk in the Sumerian King List, after Meshkiangasher and Enmerkar (1200 years, “the shepherd”); in tradition he is the father of Gilgamesh and the protagonist of Sumerian poems. His historicity is uncertain among specialists.

personas/enmerkar/resumen.texto: King of Uruk to whom tradition attributes the building of the city and campaigns against Aratta; a Sumerian poem presents him as the inventor of writing. No contemporary inscriptions.

personas/gilgamesh/resumen.texto: Hero of Mesopotamian mythology and possibly a historical king of Uruk at the beginning of the Early Dynastic period (c. 2900–2350 BC), later deified. The Sumerian poems that tell of him spread mainly under the Third Dynasty of Ur; there are no contemporary inscriptions of his.

personas/kubaba/resumen.texto: Queen of Kish who, according to the Sumerian King List, reigned a hundred years before the dynasty of Akshak. Her historicity is debated, partly because of the unusual form of the name.

personas/enmebaragesi/resumen.texto: Next-to-last king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, to which it assigns a reign of 900 years (c. 2750 BC). He is the oldest ruler in the List whose name appears in a contemporary inscription, a vessel fragment reading “Mebarasi, king of Kish” (IM 30590, provenance unknown, Baghdad Museum); another fragment, from Khafajah, may belong to a different Mebaragesi.

personas/aga-de-kish/resumen.texto: King of Kish in the Early Dynastic I period, son of Enmebaragesi according to the Sumerian King List. The Sumerian poem “Gilgamesh and Agga” tells of Kish's siege of Uruk; it is later literary tradition.

personas/mesilim/resumen.texto: King (lugal) of Kish in the Early Dynastic III period (c. 2550 BC), absent from the Sumerian King List. Inscriptions from his reign show that he sponsored works in the temples of Adab and Lagash, where he exercised a certain supremacy.

personas/puzur-suen/resumen.texto: King of Kish according to the Sumerian King List (25 years), which gives him as the son of Kug-Bau (Kubaba) and father of Ur-Zababa. It is tradition; nothing more is known about him.

personas/ur-zababa/resumen.texto: Second king of the Fourth Dynasty of Kish in the Sumerian King List, which tells that Sargon of Akkad was his cupbearer. That account is later tradition and its historical value is debated.

personas/enshakushanna/resumen.texto: King of Uruk who appears in the Sumerian King List (60 years) and who, according to his inscriptions, conquered Hamazi, Akkad, Kish and Nippur and captured Enbi-Ishtar, king of Kish; he styled himself “lord of Sumer and king of the whole land.” His chronological position is uncertain: his successor Lugal-kinishe-dudu was an ally of Entemena, around 2400 BC.

personas/lugal-kinishe-dudu/resumen.texto: King of Uruk and Ur toward the end of the 25th century BC, ally of Entemena of Lagash against Umma. His son was Lugal-kisalsi.

personas/lugal-kisalsi/resumen.texto: King of Uruk and Ur around 2400 BC, son of Lugal-kinishe-dudu according to contemporary inscriptions, although he does not appear in the Sumerian King List.

personas/lugalzagesi/resumen.texto: King of Umma and later of Uruk, the last Sumerian ruler before Sargon of Akkad; he defeated Lagash in the war over the Gu-Edin and briefly united Sumer into a single kingdom. According to the inscriptions of Sargon, the latter captured him and led him with a yoke around his neck to the gate of Enlil, in Nippur; his death is not known.

personas/meskalamdug/resumen.texto: King of the First Dynasty of Ur (26th century BC), absent from the Sumerian King List and known from a royal cylinder seal, an inscribed bead found at Mari, and perhaps his tomb PG 755 in the Royal Cemetery.

personas/puabi/resumen.texto: Woman buried in tomb PG 800 of the Royal Cemetery of Ur (c. 2590–2550 BC); her seals give her the title “nin.” It is debated whether she was a consort queen, a ruling queen or a priestess.

personas/mesannepada/resumen.texto: First king of the First Dynasty of Ur in the Sumerian King List (80 years), which says that Uruk was defeated and kingship passed to Ur. On a seal from the Royal Cemetery he also styles himself king of Kish.

personas/meskiagnun/resumen.texto: Second king of the First Dynasty of Ur according to the Sumerian King List (Mesh-ki-ang-Nanna, son of Mesannepada: 36 years, 30 in one manuscript). The inscriptions also attest A'annepada, whom the List omits.

personas/elulu/resumen.texto: Third king of the First Dynasty of Ur (25 years according to the Sumerian King List). An inscription from Eridu attributes the restoration of the ziggurat of Enki to an Elulu or Elili.

personas/balulu/resumen.texto: Last king of the First Dynasty of Ur according to the Sumerian King List (36 years); the List says that Ur was defeated and kingship passed to Awan.

personas/lugal-anne-mundu/resumen.texto: Main king of Adab, to whom the Sumerian King List assigns a reign of 90 years. There are few contemporary inscriptions; he is known mainly from a later text.

personas/ikun-shamash/resumen.texto: King of the second kingdom of Mari (around 2500 BC), probably the oldest of the three kings of Mari known from archaeology.

personas/iku-shamagan/resumen.texto: King of the second kingdom of Mari, known from an inscribed statue; he used Akkadian in his inscriptions.

personas/ishqi-mari/resumen.texto: King of the second kingdom of Mari (formerly read Lamgi-Mari), known from an inscribed statue. He died around 2330 BC.

personas/ansud/resumen.texto: King of the second kingdom of Mari, remembered for his wars against Ebla in a letter from the Mari king Enna-Dagan.

personas/iblul-il/resumen.texto: King of Mari who campaigned against Ebla in the middle Euphrates and in the upper Tigris, and asserted Mari's supremacy in northern Syria.

personas/ebih-il/resumen.texto: Superintendent (nu-banda) of Mari. His gypsum statue, dedicated to “Ishtar the virile” and found by Parrot in 1934 in the temple of Ishtar, now in the Louvre, dates from the 25th century BC.

personas/ur-nanshe/resumen.texto: Founder of the First Dynasty of Lagash (c. 2520 BC), known from inscriptions about canals and temples and for having captured Pabilgagaltuku, ruler of Umma. He was the son of Gunidu and father of Akurgal.

personas/akurgal-de-lagash/resumen.texto: Second king of the First Dynasty of Lagash, son of Ur-Nanshe and father of Eannatum (c. 2460 BC). Very little is known of his reign.

personas/eannatum/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash c. 2450 BC who defeated Umma, an event commemorated by the Stele of the Vultures, and extended his rule over much of Sumer. His inscriptions say that he subjected Elam and destroyed Susa.

personas/enannatum-i/resumen.texto: Ruler of Lagash c. 2425 BC, brother and successor of Eannatum. He fought Ur-Lumma of Umma, who had invaded Lagash; his inscriptions do not record the result, and according to the cone of Entemena the final victory belonged to his son Entemena.

personas/entemena/resumen.texto: Ruler of Lagash c. 2400 BC, son of Enannatum I, who according to his cone defeated Ur-Lumma and Il of Umma. He concluded a brotherhood pact with Lugal-kinishe-dudu of Uruk, according to the cones from Bad-tibira.

personas/enannatum-ii/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash, son of Entemena; few of his inscriptions survive, which suggests a short reign.

personas/enentarzi/resumen.texto: High priest of Ningirsu who governed Lagash after Enannatum II. An inscription tells that 600 Elamites came to plunder Lagash during his rule and were repulsed.

personas/lugalanda/resumen.texto: King of Lagash, son of Enentarzi; the inscriptions of his successor Urukagina present him as corrupt. His wife was Baranamtarra.

personas/urukagina/resumen.texto: Last king of the First Dynasty of Lagash (24th century BC), who proclaimed himself chosen by the gods and whose inscriptions record reforms. Toward the end of his reign Lagash was devastated by Lugalzagesi of Umma, and Urukagina took the title of king of Girsu.

personas/pabilgagaltuku/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Umma c. 2450 BC, captured by Ur-Nanshe of Lagash according to an inscription of the latter.

personas/ush-de-umma/resumen.texto: King or ensi of Umma c. 2450 BC. According to the cone of Entemena, he violated the border with Lagash established by Mesilim.

personas/enakalle/resumen.texto: King of Umma in the Early Dynastic III period, defeated by Eannatum of Lagash; he reigned for at least eight years.

personas/ur-lumma/resumen.texto: King of Umma, son of Enakalle, who styled himself lugal and attacked Lagash across the plain of Gu-Edin until he was defeated by Entemena, son of Enannatum I.

personas/gishakidu/resumen.texto: King of Umma, son of Il and husband of Queen Bara-irnun; he is known mainly from a votive gold plaque of his wife.

personas/bara-irnun/resumen.texto: Consort queen of Umma, wife of Gishakidu, known from a votive gold plaque on which she sets out her genealogy.

personas/sargon-de-acad/resumen.texto: Founder of the Akkadian Empire, who reigned c. 2334–2279 BC (middle chronology). He defeated Lugalzagesi and united southern Mesopotamia; his inscriptions style him “king of Kish.” His origin and rise are known from later legends.

personas/enheduanna/resumen.texto: Daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess (en) of the moon god Nanna at Ur (c. 2300 BC). Babylonian scribes of the second millennium attributed to her hymns that they copied in school; her authorship is disputed by scholars.

personas/tashlultum/resumen.texto: Wife of Sargon of Akkad, known from a single inscription on an alabaster vessel fragment dedicated to a temple by her administrator. The location of Akkad is unknown; the leading candidate is Kish.

personas/rimush/resumen.texto: Second king of Akkad, son of Sargon, who reigned c. 2279–2270 BC (middle chronology). He suppressed a rebellion led by Kaku of Ur and fought in Elam and Marhashi; according to an Old Babylonian omen, his courtiers killed him.

personas/manishtushu/resumen.texto: Third king of Akkad, son of Sargon, who reigned c. 2270–2255 BC (middle chronology). His standard inscription recounts campaigns against Anshan and Sherihum and a victory over 32 cities across the Lower Sea; according to an Old Babylonian omen, his courtiers killed him. The order between him and Rimush varies among the copies of the Sumerian King List.

personas/naram-sin-de-acad/resumen.texto: King of Akkad, grandson of Sargon, who reigned c. 2254–2218 BC (middle chronology). He defeated a great rebellion of Babylonian cities, led campaigns into northern Syria and, according to the Bassetki statue, the people of Akkad asked that he be made a god of their city. Akkad, his capital, is of unknown location in northern Babylonia; the leading candidate is Kish.

personas/shar-kali-sharri/resumen.texto: King of Akkad, son of Naram-Sin, who reigned c. 2217–2193 BC (middle chronology). His reign is the best documented in administrative tablets; his inscriptions show an empire already in decline and under pressure from the Gutians. Akkad is of unknown location; the leading candidate is Kish.

personas/ilulu/resumen.texto: One of four rivals (with Igigi, Imi and Nanum) for the throne of Akkad in the three years after the death of Shar-kali-sharri, according to the Sumerian King List. There are no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/nanum/resumen.texto: One of four rivals for the throne of Akkad after Shar-kali-sharri, according to the Sumerian King List. No inscriptions of his own.

personas/dudu-de-acad/resumen.texto: King of Akkad c. 2189–2168 BC according to the Sumerian King List (21 years; middle chronology). Some votive inscriptions and reports of campaigns are known; he was not deified.

personas/shu-turul/resumen.texto: Last king of Akkad according to the Sumerian King List (15 years, to c. 2154 BC; middle chronology), son of Dudu. He is known only from a few votive inscriptions.

personas/erridupizir/resumen.texto: Gutian ruler known from Old Babylonian copies, found at Nippur, of inscriptions on his monuments, in which he styles himself “king of Gutium, king of the four quarters” (c. 2205–2202 BC).

personas/sarlagab/resumen.texto: Second Gutian ruler in the Sumerian King List, with a reign of six years; he may have been a contemporary of Shar-kali-sharri. The Gutians made Adab their capital at the end of the Akkadian period.

personas/yarlaganda/resumen.texto: Gutian ruler who appears in the Sumerian King List as the seventeenth of his dynasty, successor of Puzur-Suen. The Gutians made Adab their capital at the end of the Akkadian period.

personas/siium/resumen.texto: Eighteenth Gutian ruler in the Sumerian King List; he is mentioned in a foundation tablet of Lugalannatum of Umma, now in the Louvre, published in 1911, which was the first contemporary witness to a Gutian king from the List. The Gutians made Adab their capital at the end of the Akkadian period.

personas/tirigan/resumen.texto: Last Gutian king in the Sumerian King List, which gives him a reign of 40 days before he was defeated by Utu-hengal of Uruk. The Gutians made Adab their capital at the end of the Akkadian period.

personas/utu-hengal/resumen.texto: King of Uruk who, according to his inscription, defeated the Gutians and ended their rule around 2112 BC. His governor of Ur, Ur-Nammu, later founded the Third Dynasty of Ur.

personas/lugalannatum/resumen.texto: Ruler (patesi) of Umma under Gutian rule around 2130 BC; a foundation tablet of his, published in 1911 and now in the Louvre, mentions the Gutian king Si'um.

personas/lugal-ushumgal/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash c. 2230–2210 BC, vassal of the Akkadian kings Naram-Sin and Shar-kali-sharri according to his seals.

personas/ur-baba/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash c. 2157–2144 BC (middle chronology), a contemporary of the last king of Akkad. Gudea was his son-in-law.

personas/gudea/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash in the Second Dynasty, active c. 2144–2124 BC according to the middle chronology (reconstructions differ by some decades). He rebuilt the Eninnu in Girsu and left inscribed statues and cylinders.

personas/ur-ningirsu/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash c. 2120 BC, son of Gudea. In the scholarly literature he is distinguished as Ur-Ningirsu II from the earlier Ur-Ningirsu.

personas/pirig-me/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash, son of Ur-Ningirsu I, whom he succeeded c. 2185–2180 BC, before Lu-Baba, Ur-Baba and Gudea. He is known from a single brick inscription and a year name.

personas/nammahani/resumen.texto: Last ensi of the Second Dynasty of Lagash (c. 2110 BC), who succeeded Ur-gar. According to the prologue of the code of Ur-Nammu, the latter killed him.

personas/ur-nammu/resumen.texto: Founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, who reigned c. 2112–2095 BC (middle chronology), with the title “king of Sumer and Akkad.” He reorganized the country, built temples and canals, and is credited with the oldest known law collection; according to a later poem, “The Death of Ur-Nammu,” he died on the battlefield (a damaged and metaphorical passage) and was not deified.

personas/shulgi/resumen.texto: Son and successor of Ur-Nammu, king of Ur c. 2094–2047 BC (middle chronology). He reorganized the administration, the calendar and writing, was deified, and conquered toward the north and the east.

personas/amar-sin/resumen.texto: Third king of the Third Dynasty of Ur, c. 2046–2038 BC (middle chronology). He campaigned in the northern and eastern regions, and his reign left very abundant administrative documentation.

personas/shu-sin/resumen.texto: Fourth king of Ur, c. 2037–2029 BC (middle chronology). He strengthened the wall against the Amorites and fought at Shimanum, Zabshali and Shimashki.

personas/ibbi-sin/resumen.texto: Last king of the Third Dynasty of Ur, c. 2028–2004 BC (middle chronology). Under his reign the kingdom broke apart; Ur fell around 2004 BC to an Elamite-led coalition.

personas/taram-uram/resumen.texto: Daughter of Apil-kin, ruler of Mari, and daughter-in-law of Ur-Nammu according to her own dedication; she was the chief wife of Shulgi in the first years of his reign, in a marriage arranged by Ur-Nammu as an alliance with Mari.

personas/shulgi-simti/resumen.texto: Wife, or rather concubine, of Shulgi who lived in Ur; she is known from the many texts of her household found in the Puzrish-Dagan archive.

personas/apil-kin/resumen.texto: Ruler (shakkanakku) of Mari after the fall of Akkad, 35 years according to the dynastic list; father of Queen Taram-Uram. His sons succeeded him.

personas/puzur-ishtar/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku of Mari, contemporary of the Third Dynasty of Ur, probably its vassal; his sons succeeded him.

personas/hanun-dagan/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku of Mari c. 2016–2008 BC, brother of Hitlal-Erra and son of Puzur-Ishtar.

personas/tish-atal/resumen.texto: Endan (king or high priest) of Urkesh under the Third Dynasty of Ur, one of the earliest known Hurrian rulers; no precise date.

personas/luh-ishan/resumen.texto: Eighth king of the dynasty of Awan, in Elam (around 2325 BC). The list of Awan places Hishep-ratep after Luh-ishan, but an inscription of Sargon calls him “son of Hishibrasini,” which is identified with Hishep-ratep; the identification and the order are uncertain.

personas/khita/resumen.texto: King of Elam, eleventh of the dynasty of Awan, who according to a treaty made peace with Naram-Sin of Akkad (around 2250 BC); probably the grandfather of Puzur-Inshushinak.

personas/puzur-inshushinak/resumen.texto: King of Elam, the last of the Awan dynasty, who declared his independence after the fall of Akkad and left inscriptions in Linear Elamite and in Akkadian. Inscriptions of Ur-Nammu say that he defeated a coalition of Kutik-Inshushinak with Tutub and Eshnunna; the synchronism is debated, and some place him as a contemporary of Naram-Sin.

personas/kindattu/resumen.texto: Sixth king of the Simashki dynasty, in Elam, a contemporary of the Third Dynasty of Ur and linked in tradition with the end of Ur.

personas/alulim/resumen.texto: First king in history according to the Sumerian King List, which places him in Eridu before the flood with a reign of thousands of years. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/alalngar/resumen.texto: Second king of Eridu according to the Sumerian King List, before the flood. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/en-men-lu-ana/resumen.texto: First king of Bad-tibira in one version of the Sumerian King List, which gives him a reign of 43,200 years. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/en-men-gal-ana/resumen.texto: Second king of Bad-tibira in some versions of the Sumerian King List, with a reign of 28,800 years. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/en-men-dur-ana/resumen.texto: King of Sippar (Zimbir), the seventh antediluvian king in the Sumerian King List. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/jushur/resumen.texto: King of Kish in the Sumerian King List, the literary composition of the beginning of the second millennium BC; for some versions he is the first king of the Kish list. A figure of tradition.

personas/kullassina-bel/resumen.texto: Second king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, with a reign of 960 years (900 in some copies). A figure of tradition.

personas/nangishlishma/resumen.texto: Third king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List. His name does not appear in Early Dynastic inscriptions; he is a figure of tradition.

personas/en-tarah-ana/resumen.texto: Fourth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/babum/resumen.texto: Fifth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List. He is unlikely to have existed: his name does not appear in texts of his time.

personas/puannum/resumen.texto: Sixth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List. He is unlikely to have existed: his name does not appear in texts of his time.

personas/kalibum/resumen.texto: Seventh king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List. His name is taken to be Akkadian, derived from “dog”; he is a figure of tradition.

personas/kalumum/resumen.texto: Eighth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, with an animal name like the kings before Etana. A figure of tradition.

personas/atab/resumen.texto: Tenth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, father of Mashda. He is unlikely to have existed: his name does not appear in texts of his time.

personas/mashda/resumen.texto: Eleventh king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, son of Atab; his name means “gazelle” in Akkadian. A figure of tradition.

personas/arwium/resumen.texto: Twelfth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, son of Mashda and predecessor of Etana. A figure of tradition.

personas/balih/resumen.texto: Fourteenth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, son and successor of Etana. He is considered a figure of tradition.

personas/melem-kish/resumen.texto: Sixteenth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, son of En-me-nuna. His name appears only in the List.

personas/barsal-nuna/resumen.texto: Seventeenth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, son of En-me-nuna and brother of Melem-Kish. His name appears only in the List.

personas/zamug/resumen.texto: Eighteenth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List, son of Barsal-nuna. His name appears only in the List.

personas/tizqar/resumen.texto: Nineteenth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to some versions of the Sumerian King List, son of Zamug. He does not appear in inscriptions of his time.

personas/ilku/resumen.texto: Twentieth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List. He does not appear in Early Dynastic inscriptions; he is unlikely to be a historical figure.

personas/iltasadum/resumen.texto: King number 21 of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List. He does not appear in Early Dynastic inscriptions; he is unlikely to be a historical figure.

personas/susuda/resumen.texto: First king of the Second Dynasty of Kish in some versions of the Sumerian King List, with a reign of 201 years. A figure of tradition.

personas/dadasig/resumen.texto: Second king of the Second Dynasty of Kish in some versions of the Sumerian King List, with a reign of 81 years. A figure of tradition.

personas/meshkiangasher/resumen.texto: First king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List, which presents him as a priest of Eanna; according to the ETCSL translation, he entered the sea and disappeared. A figure of tradition.

personas/ur-nungal/resumen.texto: Sixth king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List (30 years) and son of Gilgamesh according to it and the Tummal Chronicle. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/udul-kalama/resumen.texto: Seventh king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List; perhaps the son of Ur-Nungal and grandson of Gilgamesh. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/melem-ana/resumen.texto: Eleventh king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List, after Mesh-he. Little is known of him.

personas/lugal-kitun/resumen.texto: Last king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List, which says that Uruk was defeated and kingship passed to Ur with Mesannepada. A figure of tradition.

personas/hishep-ratep/resumen.texto: Ninth king of the dynasty of Awan, in Elam, around 2350 BC; he is identified with the Hishibrasini of the Akkadian inscriptions, named as the father of Luh-ishan, although the list of Awan places him after Luh-ishan.

personas/uhub/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Kish before Mesilim, around 2570 BC. His name is missing from the Sumerian King List, and he is known from a vessel dedicated to Zababa and a few other inscriptions.

personas/en-me-nuna/resumen.texto: Fifteenth king of the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian King List (660 years), father of Melem-Kish and Barsal-nuna. He does not appear in Early Dynastic documents; he is a figure of tradition.

personas/la-bashum/resumen.texto: Eighth king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List, with a reign of nine years. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/en-nun-tarah-ana/resumen.texto: Ninth king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List, with a reign of eight years. A figure of tradition, with no contemporary inscriptions.

personas/mesh-he/resumen.texto: Tenth king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List, which calls him “the smith” and gives him a reign of 36 years. Little is known of him, and his historicity is not established.

personas/en-sipad-zid-ana/resumen.texto: King of Larak in some versions of the Sumerian King List, with a reign of 28,800 years. He does not appear in Early Dynastic documents; he is a figure of tradition.

personas/ur-nigin/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Uruk in the 22nd century BC. According to the Sumerian King List, Akkad was defeated and kingship passed to Uruk, where Ur-nigin reigned seven years and founded a brief dynasty.

personas/ur-gigir/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Uruk in the 22nd century BC, son and successor of Ur-nigin in the Sumerian King List, in which he reigned six years.

personas/aannepada/resumen.texto: King of the First Dynasty of Ur, son of Mesannepada, whom the Sumerian King List omits. His tomb may be PG 580 in the Royal Cemetery; the date of c. 2350 BC usually given does not fit that of his father, so he is placed around 2500 BC.

personas/akalamdug/resumen.texto: Early king of the First Dynasty of Ur (26th century BC), absent from the Sumerian King List and known from his tomb (PG 1332) and an inscription from the Royal Cemetery. He may be the father or the son of Meskalamdug.

personas/ur-pabilsag/resumen.texto: Early king of the First Dynasty of Ur, absent from the Sumerian King List and known from an inscribed fragment that styles him “king of Ur.” His tomb is presumed to be PG 779 in the Royal Cemetery, the tomb of the Standard of Ur.

personas/en-hegal/resumen.texto: Possible ruler of Lagash around 2570 BC, known from a single land purchase tablet.

personas/lugalshaengur/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash around 2530 BC, tributary of Mesilim of Kish, known from the mace head that Mesilim dedicated. He was succeeded by Ur-Nanshe.

personas/baranamtarra/resumen.texto: Wife of Lugalanda of Lagash. She managed the household of the goddess Bau and her own estate, and her commercial activities are recorded in tablets from Lagash.

personas/il-de-umma/resumen.texto: King of Umma around 2420 BC who, while administrator of the temple of Zabalam, took over the government of Umma after Ur-Lumma. He was an enemy of Entemena of Lagash and the father of Gishakidu.

personas/meskigal/resumen.texto: Ruler of Adab around 2350 BC, a contemporary of Lugalzagesi and of Sargon of Akkad.

personas/nin-kisalsi/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Adab around 2500 BC who does not appear in the Sumerian King List and is known from a bowl fragment that mentions Mesilim of Kish, his probable sovereign.

personas/lugal-dalu/resumen.texto: King of Adab around 2500 BC who does not appear in the Sumerian King List and is known from an inscribed statue found in the Esar temple.

personas/puzer-mama/resumen.texto: Ruler of Lagash who took the title of king (lugal) under Shar-kali-sharri, when the Gutians had left the Akkadian kingdom greatly reduced. He begins the Second Dynasty of Lagash and died around 2200 BC.

personas/ur-ningirsu-i/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash who died around 2185 BC, known from a British Museum list of offerings that calls him “Ur-Ningirsu the elder” and from some year names. He was the father of Pirig-me.

personas/ur-gar/resumen.texto: Ruler (ensi) of Lagash, son-in-law of Ur-Baba, who succeeded Ur-Ningirsu II and was succeeded by Nammahani. He died around 2113 BC.

personas/ikun-mari/resumen.texto: King (lugal) of the second kingdom of Mari around 2500 BC, known from a stone vessel that mentions his wife Alma, who also appears in Ebla texts.

personas/saumu/resumen.texto: King (lugal) of the second kingdom of Mari, who reigned c. 2416–2400 BC. According to a letter from the Mari king Enna-Dagan, he attacked Ebla and defeated cities of the middle Euphrates.

personas/ishtup-ishar/resumen.texto: King (lugal) of the second kingdom of Mari around 2400 BC. According to Enna-Dagan's letter, he destroyed the Eblaite cities of Lalanium and Emar.

personas/ishma-dagan/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku (military governor) of Mari under Akkad, with a reign of 45 years according to the dynastic list; probably a contemporary of Shar-kali-sharri. He was succeeded by his sons Nûr-Mêr and Ishtup-Ilum.

personas/nur-mer/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku of Mari, son of Ishma-Dagan, with a reign of five years according to the dynastic list; he is known from four identical bronze votive plaques. He was succeeded by his brother Ishtup-Ilum.

personas/ishtup-ilum/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku of Mari, son of Ishma-Dagan, with a reign of 11 years according to the dynastic list; probably a contemporary of Gudea and of the Second Dynasty of Lagash.

personas/ishgum-addu/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku of Mari c. 2136–2127 BC, father of Apil-kin according to the dynastic list. No inscriptions of his are known outside it; the name could be read Ishkun-Dagan.

personas/iddi-ilum/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku of Mari, a contemporary of the Third Dynasty of Ur, probably its vassal. He is known from his headless statue, found in the royal palace of Mari.

personas/ili-ishar/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku of Mari c. 2085–2072 BC, son of Apil-kin and brother of Tura-Dagan, who succeeded him. A contemporary of the Third Dynasty of Ur, probably its vassal.

personas/tura-dagan/resumen.texto: Shakkanakku of Mari under Ur III, son of Apil-kin and brother of Ili-Ishar; he died around 2050 BC. He was probably a vassal of Ur.

personas/imta/resumen.texto: Gutian ruler, successor of Erridupizir and predecessor of Inkishush. The Gutians made Adab their capital at the end of the Akkadian period.

personas/inkishush/resumen.texto: First king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of Imta and predecessor of Sarlagab; he would have been a contemporary of Naram-Sin and Shar-kali-sharri.

personas/shulme/resumen.texto: Third king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of Sarlagab and predecessor of Elulmesh.

personas/elulmesh/resumen.texto: Fourth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List. It has been proposed that he is the same as Ilulu of Akkad; there are almost no documents from that span.

personas/inimabakesh/resumen.texto: Fifth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of Elulmesh and predecessor of Igeshaush.

personas/igeshaush/resumen.texto: Sixth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of Inimabakesh and predecessor of Yarlagab.

personas/yarlagab/resumen.texto: Seventh king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, with a reign of 15 years; he was succeeded by Ibate.

personas/ibate/resumen.texto: Eighth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, with a reign of three years (c. 2154–2151 BC). He was succeeded by Yarla.

personas/yarla/resumen.texto: Ninth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, with a reign of three years; successor of Ibate and predecessor of Kurum.

personas/kurum/resumen.texto: Tenth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of Yarla and predecessor of Apilkin.

personas/apilkin-gutio/resumen.texto: Eleventh king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of Kurum and predecessor of La-erabum. He is not the Apil-kin of Mari.

personas/la-erabum/resumen.texto: Twelfth king of the Gutian dynasty, around 2150 BC. He is one of the two Gutians with an inscription of his own, a mace head.

personas/irarum/resumen.texto: Thirteenth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of La-erabum and predecessor of Ibranum.

personas/ibranum/resumen.texto: Fourteenth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of Irarum and predecessor of Hablum.

personas/hablum/resumen.texto: Fifteenth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, successor of Ibranum and predecessor of Puzur-Suen.

personas/puzur-suen-gutio/resumen.texto: Sixteenth king of the Gutian dynasty in the Sumerian King List, son of Hablum; he is not the Puzur-Suen of Kish. He was succeeded by Yarlaganda.

personas/peli/resumen.texto: Eponymous king who founded the dynasty of Awan, in Elam, according to the Susa list; he would have reigned in the first Proto-Elamite period (c. 2400–2015 BC). He could be the first king of Awan in the Sumerian King List.

personas/tata/resumen.texto: Second king of the dynasty of Awan, in Elam, according to the Susa list, in the first Proto-Elamite period (c. 2400–2015 BC). He could be the second king of Awan in the Sumerian King List.

personas/kur-ishshak/resumen.texto: Third king of the dynasty of Awan in the Sumerian King List, in the first Proto-Elamite period (c. 2400–2015 BC). He could be the Ukku-Tanhish of the Susa list.

personas/lu-de-awan/resumen.texto: Second king of Awan in the Sumerian King List, whose name is incomplete; he could be the Tata of the Susa list. He would have reigned in the first Proto-Elamite period (c. 2400–2015 BC).

personas/eshpum/resumen.texto: Akkadian governor of Elam, c. 2269–2255 BC.

personas/epirmupi/resumen.texto: Akkadian governor (shakkanakku) of Elam and ensi of Susa. The dates given for him contradict each other (c. 2199–2154 BC or the time of Rimush and Manishtushu), so his position is uncertain.

personas/ili-ishmani/resumen.texto: Akkadian governor (shakkanakku) of Elam around 2150 BC, a contemporary of Naram-Sin or of Shar-kali-sharri; he had previously been a scribe. He probably succeeded Epirmupi.

personas/zariqum/resumen.texto: Governor (shakkanakku) of Assur under the Third Dynasty of Ur, attested from year 44 of Shulgi to year 5 of Amar-Sin (c. 2050–2041 BC). He is the only governor of the city of that period known by name.

personas/naplanum/resumen.texto: First king of Larsa c. 2025–2004 BC, according to the late Larsa list. Ur III texts mention him, but no inscription or year name of his time confirms him as king; he resided in Kisig, near Ur.

hechos/expansion-de-uruk/titulo.texto: Expansion of Uruk: Habuba Kabira, Jebel Aruda and Godin Tepe

hechos/expansion-de-uruk/resumen.texto: In the Late Uruk period, sites with material culture of Mesopotamian type arose outside Sumer: Habuba Kabira and Jebel Aruda, on the Syrian Euphrates, and a fortified enclosure at Godin Tepe, in Luristan. They are interpreted as colonies or trading posts of Uruk; the nature of that presence is debated.

hechos/vaso-de-warka/resumen.texto: Alabaster vessel found in the temple complex of Eanna, in Uruk, with reliefs in superimposed registers showing a procession of offerings before the goddess Inanna. It is dated to the level of the late Uruk or Jemdet Nasr period.

hechos/periodo-de-jemdet-nasr/resumen.texto: In the Jemdet Nasr period, proto-cuneiform administrative tablets were written outside Uruk, which shows the spread of writing in southern Mesopotamia; the mound gives its name to the period and to its painted pottery.

hechos/mascara-de-warka/resumen.texto: Female face in white marble, about 20 cm, one of the oldest known carved human faces, which perhaps represents Inanna. It is in the Iraq Museum, which recovered it undamaged after the looting of 2003.

hechos/artesa-de-uruk/resumen.texto: Stone trough with a procession of sheep in relief, found at Uruk and now in the British Museum. Together with the Warka Vase it is one of the oldest known works of narrative relief in the Near East; its meaning is unclear.

hechos/sello-cilindrico-y-cuenco-de-bord.texto: According to some sources, the cylinder seal was invented around 3500 BC in Uruk and shortly afterward in Susa, and it is linked with cuneiform writing on clay. Bevel-rim bowls, mass-produced, are the indicator of the presence of Uruk.

hechos/escritura-protoelamita/resumen.texto: A writing system used briefly in Elam before Elamite cuneiform, barely deciphered except for the numbers. It has many similarities with the proto-cuneiform tablets of Uruk IV and has been found at only five sites; most of them are at Susa.

hechos/instrucciones-de-shuruppak-primer.texto: The earliest Sumerian literary works from Abu Salabikh and Fara

Tablets from Abu Salabikh (and from Fara) of the mid-third millennium BC contain the oldest known Sumerian literary compositions: the Instructions of Shuruppak, the Hymn to the Temple of Kesh and the Zame Hymns.

hechos/primera-dinastia-de-ur/resumen.texto: Dynasty of rulers of Ur in the Early Dynastic III period, successor to the first dynasties of Kish and Uruk in the Sumerian King List. Some of its kings (Meskalamdug, Akalamdug, Ur-Pabilsag, A'annepada) are not in the List and are known from the Royal Cemetery.

hechos/cementerio-real-de-ur-entierros/t.texto: Burials in the Royal Cemetery of Ur

hechos/cementerio-real-de-ur-entierros/r.texto: The richest tombs of the Royal Cemetery, from the Early Dynastic III period, held gold and lapis lazuli grave goods and the bodies of attendants. Woolley interpreted them as voluntary sacrifices; later studies using CT scanning found signs of violent death in some skulls.

hechos/tumba-de-puabi/titulo.texto: Tomb of Puabi (PG 800) and her headdress

hechos/tumba-de-puabi/resumen.texto: Woolley found in tomb PG 800 the body of Puabi with a rich set of grave goods, among them a headdress of gold leaves, lapis lazuli and carnelian of more than 2.7 kg, and seals that give her the title “nin.” Her title (queen or priestess) is debated.

hechos/estandarte-de-ur/resumen.texto: Wooden box with a mosaic of shell, lapis lazuli and red limestone, with a war scene and a banquet scene; it came out of tomb PG 779 in 1927–1928, associated with Ur-Pabilsag, and is in the British Museum. Its function is debated.

hechos/liras-de-ur/resumen.texto: Three lyres and a harp, excavated from 1922 in the Royal Cemetery of Ur, c. 2550–2450 BC, among the oldest surviving stringed instruments. They are divided among the Iraq Museum (the bull lyre), the British Museum and the Penn Museum.
