hechos/juego-real-de-ur/resumen.texto: A race game for two players, played from the early third millennium BC; a board from the Royal Cemetery, in the British Museum, is c. 2600–2400 BC and is counted among the oldest game boards.

hechos/carnero-en-la-espesura/resumen.texto: Pair of figures of c. 2600–2400 BC excavated at Ur, one in the British Museum and another in the Penn Museum.

hechos/tesoro-de-tell-asmar/resumen.texto: Twelve votive statues found in 1933 at Eshnunna (Tell Asmar), an example of the abstract style of temple sculpture of the Early Dynastic period.

hechos/mesannepada-sobre-uruk-tradicion/.texto: The Sumerian King List says that Uruk was defeated and that kingship passed to Ur with Mesannepada, first king of its First Dynasty. Mesannepada is attested by inscriptions; the episode is known only from the List.

hechos/primera-dinastia-de-ur-cae-ante-a.texto: End of the First Dynasty of Ur before Awan (King List tradition)
The Sumerian King List tells that Ur was defeated “with weapons” and kingship passed to Awan, in Elam. There is no confirmation in contemporary sources.

hechos/aga-asedia-uruk-tradicion/titulo.texto: Agga of Kish besieges Uruk (literary tradition)

hechos/aga-asedia-uruk-tradicion/resumen.texto: The Sumerian poem “Gilgamesh and Agga” tells that Agga of Kish besieged Uruk and was defeated by Gilgamesh. It is Old Babylonian literature, and there is no contemporary evidence of the episode.

hechos/arbitraje-de-mesilim/titulo.texto: Arbitration of Mesilim between Lagash and Umma

hechos/arbitraje-de-mesilim/resumen.texto: According to Entemena, the king of Kish Mesilim fixed the border between Lagash and Umma on the plain of Gu-Edin and marked it with a stele. The exact location is unknown: the candidate is Girsu, between Girsu and Umma. Inscriptions of Mesilim also show his sponsorship of temples in Adab and Lagash.

hechos/ur-nanshe-obras-y-victoria-sobre-.texto: Ur-Nanshe: works and victory over Umma
Ur-Nanshe, first king of the First Dynasty of Lagash, left inscriptions about canals and temples, about his victory over Ur, and about the capture of Pabilgagaltuku, ruler of Umma.

hechos/guerra-entre-lagash-y-umma/titulo.texto: War between Lagash and Umma over the Gu-Edin

hechos/guerra-entre-lagash-y-umma/resume.texto: Lagash and Umma disputed for generations the fertile plain of the Gu-Edin, between Girsu and Umma (the location is Girsu); the conflict is known from Lagashite inscriptions, in particular the cone of Entemena and the Stele of the Vultures, and it ended with the conquest of Lagash by Lugalzagesi of Umma.

hechos/victoria-de-eannatum-sobre-umma/t.texto: Victory of Eannatum over Umma (Stele of the Vultures)

hechos/victoria-de-eannatum-sobre-umma/r.texto: Eannatum of Lagash defeated Ush, ruler of Umma, and the stele that commemorates him shows the battle and the imposition of a border treaty. We know it only from the Lagashite version.

hechos/eannatum-contra-elam/titulo.texto: Eannatum defeats Elam (according to his inscriptions)

hechos/eannatum-contra-elam/resumen.texto: The inscriptions of Eannatum state that he subjected Elam and destroyed Susa; there is no independent confirmation.

hechos/eannatum-extiende-su-dominio-sobr.texto: Eannatum extends his rule over Sumer (according to his inscriptions)
The inscriptions of Eannatum say that he subjected much of Sumer and Akkad; only the Lagashite version is known.

hechos/lagash-contra-ur-lumma-de-umma/ti.texto: Lagash against Ur-Lumma of Umma: the victory of Entemena

hechos/lagash-contra-ur-lumma-de-umma/re.texto: Ur-Lumma invaded Lagash across the Gu-Edin and burned the stele of Eannatum; Enannatum I fought him, but according to the cone of Entemena the victory and the death of Ur-Lumma in Umma were Entemena's. Il, who succeeded him, attacked again.

hechos/entemena-derrota-a-il-de-umma/res.texto: Entemena defeated Il of Umma over the border; the result was recorded in the cone of Entemena.

hechos/pacto-de-hermandad-de-entemena-y-.texto: Brotherhood pact between Entemena and Lugal-kinishe-dudu
Cones from the Emush temple record that Entemena of Lagash and Lugal-kinishe-dudu of Uruk established a brotherhood pact between them.

hechos/reformas-de-urukagina-hecho/resum.texto: Urukagina of Lagash, who assumed kingship as the chosen of the gods, had reforms recorded against abuses by officials and priests. The scope of these reforms is debated, and so is whether what he proclaimed was “freedom.”

hechos/lugalzagesi-conquista-lagash/resu.texto: Toward the end of the reign of Urukagina, Lugalzagesi of Umma attacked and devastated Lagash, especially its sacred places; Urukagina withdrew to Girsu and took the title of king of Girsu. A lament blames Lugalzagesi and not Urukagina.

hechos/lugalzagesi-reina-en-uruk/resumen.texto: Lugalzagesi, king of Umma and later of Uruk, briefly united Sumer into a single kingdom; he was the last Sumerian king before the conquest of Sargon of Akkad.

hechos/hegemonia-de-enshakushanna-de-uru.texto: According to his inscriptions, Enshakushanna of Uruk conquered Hamazi, Akkad, Kish and Nippur and captured Enbi-Ishtar, king of Kish. His chronological position is uncertain, because his successor Lugal-kinishe-dudu was an ally of Entemena around 2400 BC.

hechos/sargon-derrota-a-lugalzagesi/resu.texto: According to the inscription of Sargon, he defeated Uruk, tore down its walls, captured Lugalzagesi and led him with a yoke around his neck to the gate of Enlil, in Nippur. It is dated to around 2300 BC; Sallaberger and Schrakamp propose 2292.

hechos/sargon-rey-de-acad/resumen.texto: Sargon ascends the throne of Akkad, a city of unknown location in northern Babylonia (the location is Kish, whose royal title he also used). According to later tradition he had been cupbearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish; that account is legendary. The unification of the south came later.

hechos/sargon-en-tuttul/titulo.texto: Sargon at Tuttul: the Upper Land given to him by Dagan

hechos/sargon-en-tuttul/resumen.texto: An inscription of Sargon says that he paid homage to Dagan at Tuttul, who gave him the Upper Land: Mari, Yarmuti and Ebla, as far as the Cedar Forest and the Silver Mountains. The “Upper Sea” appears in other formulas and is attributed separately.

hechos/sargon-en-elam-y-marhashi/titulo.texto: Campaigns of Sargon in Elam and Marhashi

hechos/sargon-en-elam-y-marhashi/resumen.texto: Year names and copies of inscriptions recall that Sargon defeated Elam, Marhashi and Urua, and conquered Simurrum.

hechos/barcos-de-dilmun-magan-y-meluhha-.texto: Ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun at the quay of Akkad

An inscription attributed to Sargon says that he moored at the quay of Akkad ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun; it is used as evidence of Akkadian trade with the Gulf and the Indus valley. Akkad is of unknown location; the location is Kish.

hechos/enheduanna-suma-sacerdotisa-de-na.texto: Enheduanna, high priestess of Nanna at Ur
Sargon appointed his daughter Enheduanna as high priestess of the moon god at Ur, an office that later school tradition associated with the hymns attributed to her.

hechos/rebelion-de-kaku-de-ur-contra-rim.texto: Revolt of Kaku of Ur against Rimush
On taking the throne, Rimush faced a revolt led by Kaku of Ur, which brought together Adab, Lagash, Zabalam and Kazallu. Rimush suppressed it.

hechos/rimush-contra-elam-y-marhashi/tit.texto: Rimush wages war in Elam, Awan and Marhashi

hechos/rimush-contra-elam-y-marhashi/res.texto: Inscriptions of Rimush recount campaigns on the Iranian plateau, in Elam, Awan and Marhashi.

hechos/manishtushu-en-anshan-y-sherihum/.texto: According to his standard inscription, Manishtushu defeated Anshan and Sherihum and thirty-two cities across the Lower Sea, which he reached by ship. That these were Magan is an interpretation.

hechos/obelisco-de-manishtushu-compras-d.texto: The diorite obelisk records land purchases by the king and the names of the officials (“sons of Akkad”) who witnessed them. It is believed to come from Sippar and the lands were in northern Babylonia; the location is Kish.

hechos/naram-sin-reconstruye-el-ekur/tit.texto: Naram-Sin rebuilds the Ekur and the walls of Nippur

hechos/naram-sin-reconstruye-el-ekur/res.texto: Naram-Sin rebuilt the Ekur temple and the walls of Nippur, 17.5 metres wide.

hechos/naram-sin-contra-armanum-y-ebla/r.texto: The conquest of Armanum and Ebla is known from a year name and from an Old Babylonian copy of a statue inscription found at Ur. Sargon had already defeated Ebla.

hechos/naram-sin-contra-manium-de-magan/.texto: Naram-Sin defeated Manium, king of Magan, a country of southeastern Arabia (Oman and the United Arab Emirates). The place of the battle is unknown; the location is Hili, a site in that region with occupation of the period.

hechos/gran-revuelta-contra-naram-sin/re.texto: A great rebellion, led by Iphur-Kish of Kish and Amar-girid of Uruk, with Enlil-nizu of Nippur, Kutha, Sippar, Kazallu, Apiak and other cities, came close to succeeding but was defeated. The inscription recounts that Naram-Sin won nine battles in one year.

hechos/naram-sin-es-deificado/titulo.texto: Naram-Sin is made god of Akkad

hechos/naram-sin-es-deificado/resumen.texto: According to the inscription on the Bassetki statue, after defeating the revolt the people of Akkad asked the gods that Naram-Sin be god of their city and erected his statue; his name is written with the sign that marks gods.

hechos/naram-sin-sobre-los-lullubi/resum.texto: The victory stele shows Naram-Sin on the mountain, wearing a horned crown, defeating the Lullubi of the Zagros. The place of the battle is unknown; the location is Halabja, in Lullubi country.

hechos/naram-sin-en-las-fuentes-del-tigr.texto: Naram-Sin at the sources of the Tigris and the Euphrates
Naram-Sin commemorated in a year name having reached the sources of the Tigris and the Euphrates; a stele of his was found at Pir Hüseyin, near Diyarbakır (the location is the city).

hechos/palacio-de-naram-sin-en-tell-brak.texto: Palace of Naram-Sin at Tell Brak

At Tell Brak, on the Khabur, a large building was excavated, called the palace of Naram-Sin, with foundation bricks bearing his name. It was more a fortress or a store for tribute than a residence, and it attests the Akkadian presence in the north.

hechos/tratado-de-naram-sin-y-hita/titul.texto: Treaty between Naram-Sin and Hita of Elam

hechos/tratado-de-naram-sin-y-hita/resum.texto: An Elamite tablet found at Susa records a peace agreement between Naram-Sin and a king of Awan, invoking the gods of both countries as witnesses.

hechos/cabeza-de-ninive/resumen.texto: Head of copper alloy representing a king, found in 1931 in the temple of Ishtar at Nineveh; specialists attribute it to Sargon, Manishtushu or Naram-Sin, and it is an example of the attention to detail in Akkadian art.

hechos/acad-pone-gobernadores-en-susa/re.texto: The kings of Akkad ruled Elam through governors (shakkanakku) based at Susa: Eshpum, Epirmupi and Ili-ishmani. Epirmupi is placed uncertainly, between Rimush and Shar-kali-sharri.

hechos/maldicion-de-acad-y-el-ekur/titul.texto: Naram-Sin and the Ekur in the Curse of Akkad

hechos/maldicion-de-acad-y-el-ekur/resum.texto: The Sumerian poem says that Naram-Sin offended Enlil at Nippur and that the god, in punishment, sent the Gutians against Akkad. It is a theological explanation written afterward; the inscriptions of the period say, on the contrary, that Naram-Sin rebuilt the Ekur and the walls of Nippur.

hechos/fin-del-imperio-acadio/resumen.texto: After Shar-kali-sharri the kingdom was reduced to northern Babylonia, with rival kings; Dudu and Shu-turul held it together for some decades. The causes are debated: Gutian invasions according to tradition, climate, revolts of the cities. Akkad is of unknown location; the location is Kish.

hechos/gutios-dominan-sumer/resumen.texto: The Gutians, a people of the western Zagros, made Adab their capital at the end of the Akkadian period, and their rulers reigned over part of Sumer; the Sumerian King List attributes a series of kings to them. The only royal Gutian inscriptions are those of Erridupizir and the mace of La-erabum; the violent invasion recounted by tradition is viewed with skepticism today.

hechos/gudea-reconstruye-el-eninnu/resum.texto: Gudea rebuilt the Eninnu, the temple of Ningirsu at Girsu, and left an account of the work on two clay cylinders.

hechos/utu-hengal-derrota-a-tirigan/titu.texto: Utu-hengal defeats Tirigan and ends Gutian rule

hechos/utu-hengal-derrota-a-tirigan/resu.texto: According to his inscription, the envoys of Utu-hengal of Uruk captured Tirigan, the last Gutian king, with his wife and children at Dabrum, and he put his foot on his neck before Utu. The King List gives him a reign of 40 days. The place of the capture is unknown; the location is Uruk, where the stele stood.

hechos/ur-nammu-funda-la-tercera-dinasti.texto: Ur-Nammu founds the Third Dynasty of Ur

Ur-Nammu, governor of Ur under Utu-hengal, succeeded him and founded the Third Dynasty of Ur with the title “king of Sumer and Akkad.” A much later Babylonian tradition tells that Utu-hengal died in an accident while inspecting a dyke; other authors believe he was deposed by notables led by Ur-Nammu, probably his brother.

hechos/ur-nammu-corona-en-nippur/titulo.texto: Ur-Nammu is recognized at a coronation in Nippur

hechos/ur-nammu-corona-en-nippur/resumen.texto: Ur-Nammu was recognized as regional ruler of Ur, Eridu and Uruk at a coronation in Nippur.

hechos/ur-nammu-conquista-lagash/resumen.texto: According to the prologue of his code, Ur-Nammu killed Nammahani, the last ensi of Lagash, and defeated his former lord at Uruk.

hechos/ur-nammu-derrota-a-puzur-inshushi.texto: Ur-Nammu defeats a coalition of Kutik-Inshushinak

Inscriptions of Ur-Nammu say he defeated a coalition of Kutik-Inshushinak (Puzur-Inshushinak) with Tutub and Eshnunna. The synchronism is debated: some make Puzur-Inshushinak a contemporary of Naram-Sin. In the middle chronology Gudea had already died; only the chronologies that shorten the Gutian period would allow an overlap.

hechos/puzur-inshushinak-ataca-acad/resu.texto: After the fall of Akkad, Puzur-Inshushinak of Elam raided northern Babylonia; Ur-Nammu names among the cities taken from him Eshnunna and Tutub, and the location is Eshnunna.

hechos/ur-nammu-cava-el-canal-iturungal/.texto: A cone attributed to Bad-tibira records that Ur-Nammu, king of Ur and of the lands of Sumer and Akkad, dug the Iturungal canal for Inanna.

hechos/codigo-de-ur-nammu-hecho/resumen.texto: The collection of laws attributed to Ur-Nammu (or to Shulgi) is the oldest known law collection today and sets silver penalties for several crimes.

hechos/zigurat-de-ur-construccion/titulo.texto: Construction of the ziggurat of Ur

hechos/zigurat-de-ur-construccion/resume.texto: Ur-Nammu began the work on the ziggurat of the temple of Nanna at Ur, later restored by Nabonidus. The ziggurats of Nippur, Uruk and Eridu are also associated with the period of the Third Dynasty of Ur.

hechos/muerte-de-ur-nammu/resumen.texto: According to a later poem, “The Death of Ur-Nammu,” he died on the battlefield after being abandoned by his army; the passage is damaged and metaphorical. The place is unknown; the location is Ur, where his burial is recounted. His son Shulgi succeeded him.

hechos/estela-de-ur-nammu-hecho/resumen.texto: Limestone stele found in fragments in 1925 in the precinct of Nanna at Ur, with reliefs on both faces; its reconstruction is debated.

hechos/shulgi-toma-der/resumen.texto: After the 20th year of his reign, Shulgi took Der, a border city with Elam that controlled a route into the Zagros, and continued with campaigns in Karahar, Simurrum and Harshi.

hechos/matrimonios-de-las-hijas-de-shulg.texto: Marriages of Shulgi's daughters to rulers of Marhashi, Anshan and Pashime
Shulgi's year 18 records the marriage of a daughter to the king of Marhashi, and year 30 that of another princess to the ruler of Anshan; Taram-Shulgi married Shudda-bani of Pashime.

hechos/reformas-administrativas-de-shulg.texto: In the second half of his reign (according to Steinkeller, after the first 20 years) Shulgi reorganized the army, the tax system (the bala), the administration of temple lands, the training of scribes and the royal calendar, and was deified; Waetzoldt and Sallaberger debate some of the measures.

hechos/puzrish-dagan-fundacion/resumen.texto: Shulgi founded the administrative center of Puzrish-Dagan near Nippur, which received and distributed the livestock of the bala; the texts begin in year 26 of his reign, around 2069 BC.

hechos/muralla-de-shulgi-contra-los-amor.texto: In year 37 of Shulgi a great defensive wall was raised in the north against the raids of the Amorites (Martu); its course is unknown, and the location is Sippar, at the northern end of the kingdom.

hechos/campanas-de-shulgi-en-el-zagros/t.texto: Campaigns of Shulgi in the upper Tigris and the Zagros

hechos/campanas-de-shulgi-en-el-zagros/r.texto: According to the year names, years 24–32 are campaigns against Karahar, Simurrum and Harshi, years 34–35 against Anshan, and years 44–48 against Lullubum, Urbilum, Shashrum, Arraphum, Simurrum, Karahar, Kimash, Hurti and Harshi. The location is Urbilum, one of the cities named.

hechos/matrimonio-de-shulgi-con-taram-ur.texto: Marriage of Shulgi to Taram-Uram of Mari
Taram-Uram, daughter of Apil-kin of Mari and daughter-in-law of Ur-Nammu according to her dedication, married Shulgi, in an alliance arranged by Ur-Nammu before his death, around 2095 BC.

hechos/campanas-de-amar-sin/titulo.texto: Campaigns of Amar-Sin in the north and the east

hechos/campanas-de-amar-sin/resumen.texto: According to the year names, Amar-Sin destroyed Harshi and Kimash (year 1), Urbilum (year 2), Shashrum and Shurudhum (year 6), and Bitum-rabium, Jabru and Huhnuri (year 7). The location is Urbilum.

hechos/shu-sin-destruye-shimanum/resumen.texto: Shu-Sin had given his daughter in marriage to the ruler of Shimanum; he rebelled, Shu-Sin destroyed the city (year 3) and settled the prisoners near Nippur, where he founded a new Shimanum. The site of the city is unknown; the location is Nippur.

hechos/shu-sin-refuerza-la-muralla/titul.texto: Shu-Sin reinforces the wall against the Amorites

hechos/shu-sin-refuerza-la-muralla/resum.texto: In year 4 of Shu-Sin a wall was built between the Euphrates and the Tigris against the raids of the Amorites. Its course is unknown; the location is Sippar, at the northern end of the kingdom.

hechos/ibbi-sin-fortifica-ur-y-nippur/re.texto: In year 6 of Ibbi-Sin the great walls of Nippur and Ur were built, which were not enough to stop the raids or to keep the kingdom together.

hechos/nombres-de-ano-de-ibbi-sin/resume.texto: The year names of Ibbi-Sin record the destruction of Simurrum (year 3), the marriage of his daughter to the ruler of Zabshali (year 5), a campaign against Huhnuri (year 9), the defeat of Susa, Adamdun and Awan (year 14), and the submission of the Amorites (year 17).

hechos/carestia-de-grano-bajo-ibbi-sin/t.texto: Rise in the price of grain under Ibbi-Sin

hechos/carestia-de-grano-bajo-ibbi-sin/r.texto: In the seventh and eighth years of Ibbi-Sin the price of grain rose sixtyfold over the normal price. It is linked to the Amorite raids, drought and the crisis of the agricultural system.

hechos/naplanum-se-independiza-en-larsa/.texto: According to the late list of Larsa, Naplanum was the first king of Larsa around 2025 BC; no inscription or year name of his time confirms it, and Larsa remained within the kingdom of Ibbi-Sin.

hechos/disolucion-del-reino-de-ur-iii/ti.texto: Breakup of the kingdom of Ur under Ibbi-Sin

hechos/disolucion-del-reino-de-ur-iii/re.texto: Under Ibbi-Sin the central provinces became independent, among them Eshnunna and Isin with Ishbi-Erra. The archives of the major centers stop from the third year of his reign, and there are signs of famine.

hechos/caida-de-ur-ante-elam/resumen.texto: Around 2004 BC a coalition of Shimashki and Elam took Ur; the Lament for Sumer and Ur says that Ibbi-Sin was led in chains to Elam. That the Elamite king was Kindattu is attested in the list of Shilhak-Inshushinak and in a hymn to Ishbi-Erra; according to a year name of the latter, in his year 16 he defeated the Elamites.

hechos/segundo-reino-de-mari/resumen.texto: The second kingdom of Mari was ruled by kings (lugal) known from statues and votive objects, among them Ikun-Shamash, Iku-Shamagan and Ishqi-Mari; its chronology is very uncertain.

hechos/unidades-de-medida-mesopotamicas/.texto: Each city had its own measures in the Early Dynastic period; under Sargon a common standard was set, which Naram-Sin improved and which Ur III took up with the hymn to Nanshe, and the prologue of the code of Ur-Nammu mentions reforms of weights and measures.

hechos/sistema-sexagesimal/resumen.texto: The base-60 numeral system originated among the Sumerians in the third millennium BC and was inherited by the Babylonians; it is still used in modified form for time, angles and coordinates.

lugares/ur/resumen.texto: Sumerian city at present-day Tell el-Muqayyar, occupied since the Ubaid period. It was the seat of the First Dynasty of Ur and, with Ur-Nammu, the capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur; the site was abandoned in the Neo-Babylonian or Persian period.

lugares/cementerio-real-de-ur/resumen.texto: Necropolis of Ur, with about 1850 tombs excavated by Woolley between 1922 and 1934; the richest are from the Early Dynastic III period, with gold grave goods, lapis lazuli and buried attendants. Puabi's is PG 800.

lugares/zigurat-de-ur/resumen.texto: Ziggurat of the temple of Nanna, moon god of Ur, raised by Ur-Nammu around 2100 BC and later restored, in the Neo-Babylonian period, by Nabonidus.

lugares/lagash/resumen.texto: City-state of southern Sumer, at present-day Al-Hiba. Its First Dynasty and the Second Dynasty of Gudea are known from inscriptions; the level from the Early Dynastic period to Ur III is the best excavated.

lugares/girsu/resumen.texto: Religious center of the state of Lagash, at present-day Tell Telloh, with the temple of Ningirsu (Eninnu). There was a Hellenistic and Parthian reoccupation. Its excavations yielded statues of Gudea and thousands of administrative tablets.

lugares/eninnu/resumen.texto: Temple of Ningirsu at Girsu. Inscribed bricks name Ur-Nanshe and Eannatum, but most are from the restoration of Gudea, whose cylinders describe the work.

lugares/umma/resumen.texto: Sumerian city at Tell Jokha; part of the scholarship places the Umma of the Early Dynastic III period at Umm al-Aqarib, 7 km away. Its long border dispute with Lagash over the Gu-Edin is documented by inscriptions of Entemena; under the Third Dynasty of Ur it was a provincial center with more than 30,000 tablets.

lugares/kish/resumen.texto: City of northern Sumer, seat of several dynasties in the Sumerian King List. Its kings styled themselves “king of Kish” as a claim to supremacy, a title that Sargon of Akkad also used.

lugares/nippur/resumen.texto: Holy city of Enlil, at present-day Nuffar, the religious center of Sumer. There stood the Ekur; kings of Akkad and Ur dedicated objects in its sanctuary.

lugares/ekur/resumen.texto: Temple of Enlil in Nippur, the center of the cult of the chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon; the rulers of Mesopotamia mention it in their inscriptions.

lugares/eridu/resumen.texto: Sumerian city at Tell Abu Shahrain, seat of the cult of Enki. The Sumerian King List presents it as the first city with kingship; the ziggurat of Ur-Nammu is later.

lugares/shuruppak/resumen.texto: City in central Sumer, today Tell Fara. Tablets from the Early Dynastic III period came from it, among them literary and lexical texts; tradition links it to Ziusudra and Ubara-Tutu.

lugares/adab/resumen.texto: Sumerian city at Tell Bismaya, between Girsu and Nippur. Its most important king, Lugal-Anne-Mundu, appears in the Sumerian King List; at the end of the Akkadian period it was the capital of the Gutians.

lugares/tell-asmar/resumen.texto: City of the Diyala valley, occupied since the Jemdet Nasr period. In the Early Dynastic period the temple of Abu and the hoard of votive statues were found there; under Ur III it was a provincial center.

lugares/khafajah/resumen.texto: Site of the Diyala, ancient Tutub, occupied since the Uruk and Jemdet Nasr periods; its Early Dynastic temples are known from the excavations of the Oriental Institute of Chicago.

lugares/tell-agrab/resumen.texto: Mound of the Diyala valley with occupation from Jemdet Nasr and the Early Dynastic period until the end of the third millennium; a temple with votive statues was found there.

lugares/tell-al-ubaid/resumen.texto: Small site about 7 km from Ur, eponym of the Ubaid period. It also has a temple and a cemetery of the Early Dynastic period.

lugares/abu-salabikh/resumen.texto: Sumerian city about 20 km from Nippur, whose main occupation reaches the Early Dynastic III period; of the Akkadian or Ur III periods there are only potsherds in a well, without levels. Its Early Dynastic tablets include literary texts, such as the Instructions of Shuruppak.

lugares/jemdet-nasr/resumen.texto: Mound at present-day Babil, eponym of the Jemdet Nasr period (c. 3100–2900 BC). Proto-cuneiform tablets and characteristic painted pottery come from it.

lugares/tell-uqair/resumen.texto: Mound about 25 km NNE of Kish, just north of Kutha, with a painted temple of the Uruk period (the “Painted Temple”) and occupation from the Ubaid period.

lugares/kutha/resumen.texto: City of central Mesopotamia (Tell Ibrahim), occupied from the Akkadian period to the Hellenistic era. Nergal was worshipped there.

lugares/zabalam/resumen.texto: Sumerian city (Tell Ibzaykh), seat of a cult of Inanna. Rimush's inscriptions name it among the rebel cities.

lugares/bad-tibira/resumen.texto: Antediluvian Sumerian city in the Sumerian King List (Tell al-Madina), occupied until c. 1500 BC. Entemena and Ur-Nammu carried out works there.

lugares/sippar/resumen.texto: City of northern Babylonia on the Euphrates, with the temple of Utu/Shamash. It appears among the cities that supported the rebellion against Naram-Sin.

lugares/marad/resumen.texto: City of central Mesopotamia (Tell Wannat es-Sadum) with the cult of Lugal-Marda; its texts are mostly from the Old Babylonian period.

lugares/kisurra/resumen.texto: City north of Shuruppak (today Abu Hatab), subordinate to Uruk, Isin and Larsa.

lugares/puzrish-dagan/resumen.texto: Administrative center founded by Shulgi, near Nippur, to receive and redistribute livestock and other goods; its archives are key to the taxation system of the Third Dynasty of Ur.

lugares/tell-brak/resumen.texto: Ancient Nagar, a city of the upper Khabur (Syria) with occupation from the Halaf period. Under Naram-Sin a large Akkadian building with bricks bearing his name was erected there.

lugares/tell-leilan/resumen.texto: Site on the Khabur (Syria), known at the end of the third millennium as Shekhna. It was an administrative center under the Akkadian Empire; its abandonment around 2200 BC is linked in the scholarship to the 4.2 ka climate event.

lugares/habuba-kabira/resumen.texto: City founded on the Syrian Euphrates in the Late Uruk period and occupied for about 120 years; its layout and material culture are of southern type, which is interpreted as a colony of Uruk.

lugares/jebel-aruda/resumen.texto: Fortified site on the west bank of the Euphrates (Syria), founded on virgin soil in the Uruk V period; it is interpreted as an outpost linked to the expansion of Uruk.

lugares/godin-tepe/resumen.texto: Site in Luristan (western Iran) with a fortified settlement of the Late Uruk period (c. 3200–3000 BC), considered a trading post of Mesopotamian networks.

lugares/hamoukar/resumen.texto: Large site of the Syrian Jazira, an urban center from the beginning of the 4th millennium BC, destroyed around 3500 BC in what may be the oldest evidence of urban warfare in the Near East; the destruction predates the start of the timeline.

lugares/tell-chuera/resumen.texto: City of northern Syria, important in the Early Dynastic period and abandoned around 2300 BC for unknown reasons.

lugares/tell-beydar/resumen.texto: Ancient Nabada, on the Syrian Khabur; in the mid-third millennium it was a regional center with tablet archives. After its abandonment it was reoccupied around 1400 BC and in the Neo-Assyrian and Hellenistic periods.

lugares/urkesh/resumen.texto: Hurrian city of the Khabur (Tell Mozan), occupied from the third millennium; its endan Tish-atal ruled in the time of the Third Dynasty of Ur.

lugares/eanna/resumen.texto: Great temple complex of Uruk, residence of Inanna, built from the Uruk period and the economic and administrative center of the city. It was one of the most influential sanctuaries of Mesopotamia.

lugares/mari/resumen.texto: Semitic city-state on the Euphrates, at present-day Tell Hariri (Syria), which flourished between c. 2900 and 1759 BC. It was abandoned in the mid-26th century BC and rebuilt before 2500 BC as the capital of a second kingdom; under Akkad and Ur III it was governed by shakkanakku.

lugares/isin/resumen.texto: City occupied since the late 4th millennium BC (Uruk period), about 40 km southeast of Al Diwaniyah, with the cult of the healing goddess Gula. It was the capital of the dynasty of Ishbi-Erra.

lugares/larsa/resumen.texto: City-state of Sumer, center of the cult of the sun god Utu with the temple E-babbar, about 25 km southeast of Uruk. Eannatum of Lagash already mentions it in the Early Dynastic period, and Naplanum was its first king according to the late list of Larsa.

lugares/der/resumen.texto: Sumerian city-state east of the Tigris, on the border with Elam, next to al-Badra, with the god Ishtaran. Shulgi took it in the years after his 20th year of reign.

lugares/apiak/resumen.texto: City between Kish and Marad, on the Abgal canal, active from the Akkadian period to Isin-Larsa. Its exact location is uncertain.

lugares/tell-al-wilayah/resumen.texto: Site in eastern Iraq, about 20 km southwest of Kut, occupied from the Early Dynastic period to Ur III, with a large building of the Akkadian period. Looting after 2003 damaged it greatly.

lugares/tell-taya/resumen.texto: Site about 20 km southwest of Mosul, intermittently occupied in the second half of the third millennium BC and in later periods, with a wall and a central mound.

lugares/tepe-gawra/resumen.texto: Settlement about 24 km NNE of Mosul, occupied between c. 5000 and 1500 BC, with levels of the Halaf, Ubaid and Uruk periods (4000–3100 BC).

lugares/nuzi/resumen.texto: City about 12 km southwest of Kirkuk, occupied since the Ubaid period; in the Akkadian period it was called Gasur and gained importance, and it regained it under Mitanni.

lugares/terqa/resumen.texto: City of the middle Euphrates, about 64 km north of Mari, near the mouth of the Khabur. The Akkadian Empire controlled it in Early Bronze IV, and Ur III may have held it under its governors of Mari.

lugares/tuttul/resumen.texto: City at the confluence of the Balikh and the Euphrates, near Raqqa, which Sargon of Akkad visited to pay homage to Dagan according to one of his inscriptions.

lugares/tell-arbid/resumen.texto: City of the Khabur (Syria), densely populated in the first half of the third millennium BC, especially in the Ninevite 5 period, with temples and residential quarters; there are fewer finds from the Akkadian period.

lugares/chagar-bazar/resumen.texto: Mound on the Khabur (Syria), near Tell Brak, occupied from the Halaf period to the mid-second millennium BC.

lugares/qalat-al-bahrain/resumen.texto: Artificial mound of seven layers in Bahrain, with remains from 2300 BC, which was the capital of the Dilmun civilization and is the oldest fortification in the Persian Gulf.

lugares/hili/resumen.texto: The largest Bronze Age site in the United Arab Emirates, from the third millennium BC, in the region of Magan; its oldest settlement (Hili 8) dates to c. 3000 BC, with the earliest traces of oasis agriculture in southeastern Arabia.

lugares/borsippa/resumen.texto: City southwest of Babylon, on the east bank of the Euphrates, with the cult of Tutu. In the Ur III period its governor was Puzur-Tutu, who at the end supported Ishbi-Erra; if the BAR.KI of Naram-Sin's inscriptions is Borsippa, it took part in the rebellion against him, although that identification is debated.

lugares/dilbat/resumen.texto: City about 25 km south of Babylon, founded in the Early Dynastic III period and occupied in the Akkadian, Old Babylonian, Kassite, Sasanian and early Islamic periods. Its ziggurat was that of Urash.
